https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/cele.title: ‘We’re not criminals’: what Just Stop Oil’s poster girls told me
https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/cele.text:
Whatever you think of Phoebe Plummer and Anna Holland’s decision to throw soup at one of the world’s most famous paintings, it is undeniable that their act of eco-protest has had an unusual cut-through.
The two Just Stop Oil activists are likely to be given jail terms in September after being found guilty of criminal damage for throwing the contents of two tins of tomato soup over Vincent van Gogh’s Sunflowers in the National Gallery in London.
When I met them a few days after the incident, which made headlines around the world in October 2022, they were far from contrite and planning further protests. And, perhaps because of Plummer’s pink hair, they were immediately recognisable.
As the two students left the café in southeast London where we had been talking, staff and customers gave them astonished looks. “Oh my God, I’ve just realised who they are,” said one of the female baristas, as if she’d just clocked Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce. “Sidcup is a good place to lie low,” added one of her customers.
Plummer and Holland, both 22, were told by Judge Christopher Hehir at Southwark Crown Court last week to be “prepared in practical and emotional terms to go to prison”. The same judge earlier this month sentenced five JSO activists to jail terms of between four and five years for protests that brought part of the M25 to a standstill over four days in 2022.
Plummer has already been jailed for six months for her part in a slow march in London, and when I spoke to the two women they were familiar with custody cells after their arrest for the soup throwing and breezily sought to put a positive spin on the experience. “I bring my university reading into jail cells with me because I’ve got time to study,” said Holland, who was studying English literature and creative writing at Newcastle University at the time.
• Just Stop Oil sentences will only strengthen resolve, jailed founder believes
“They’re not pleasant places to be, but in a custody cell you get hot food, shelter, clean clothes, warm blankets; things that aren’t guaranteed if we keep on hurtling towards climate catastrophe. Millions in the global south have already lost these things to climate disaster,” said Plummer, who studied social anthropology at Soas, University of London.
Plummer said she felt “empowered” after throwing the soup at Sunflowers. “I felt like I was seizing back power from the systems that are hell-bent on destroying us and destroying everything we know and love. I felt like I was grabbing power over my future because right now we’re being denied our right to a future.”
She has become the “poster girl” for JSO, involved in several protests and stunts. The pair warned then that their attention-grabbing at the National Gallery was the start of an escalation of protests by Just Stop Oil, which is trying to disrupt airports during the holiday season, including Gatwick where several activists were arrested yesterday.
Throwing the soup caused outrage around the world. Some of the disgust dissipated once it became clear that the painting had a glass cover and the work was undamaged. But nevertheless there was widespread feeling that vigorously thrusting a can of soup so close to one of the country’s greatest art treasures was pretty idiotic.
• Prepare for jail, judge tells Just Stop Oil’s Van Gogh protesters
Judge Hehir said they “came within the width of a pane of glass of destroying one of the most valuable artworks in the world”. The frame of the painting was damaged in the attack. Copycat incidents have included pumpkin soup being thrown at Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa in the Louvre in Paris in January this year.
Plummer and Holland said they wanted to do something that would deliver a visual jolt. “It was a very shocking action,” Holland said. “We did this to shock people because once people were shocked at what we did, we wanted them to start asking themselves: where should that shock truly be directed?”
The Sunflowers is “so iconic”, Plummer chipped in. They needed to get people’s attention, they claimed, to try to engage them on the peril facing those affected by climate change, including people displaced by floods in Pakistan, suffering from famine in Somalia and dying from the heatwave we had in Britain that summer. “Two young girls throwing soup at a painting has gotten people talking about it more than these millions of lives that have been destroyed due to climate catastrophes,” Plummer said.
They may have been exaggerating, but it is probably true that more people were aware of their stunt than the tragedy developing in Somalia. However, targeting one of the world’s most famous paintings caused enormous upset and I wondered why they targeted a genius who found a whole new way to show us the natural world that he loved.
“That painting was protected by glass,” Plummer said. “But the fact is millions of people in the global south aren’t protected. As young people our own futures aren’t protected. That shock reaction is because it is something beautiful, and you have that feeling of wanting to protect something beautiful, something valuable, of not wanting to see it be destroyed. Where is that sentiment when it’s our planet? When it’s our environment? When it’s people whose lives are being destroyed?”
This is where a lot of people will part company with Just Stop Oil. People do care about the planet. It is possible to sympathise with the view that climate change is not being tackled with sufficient urgency while taking a hardline stance on soup in art galleries. Isn’t the danger for those who throw soup, glue themselves to walls and endlessly block traffic that their actions alienate their audience?
“I completely understand people’s frustrations against us,” Holland said. “But the fact of the matter is, as a result of our action, people are talking about not just what we did, but about the demands that we are conveying as Just Stop Oil.”
Were they? Or were they just talking about the outrageousness? “Well, this isn’t a popularity contest. We’re trying to make change. Martin Luther King was the most hated man in America when he was alive. The suffragettes weren’t popular,” Plummer said.
Some of the comment on Just Stop Oil has been that “posh” people with plummy accents are disrupting the lives of less privileged people. Everyone, regardless of class, gender or ethnicity, would be affected by the climate crisis and so it is unifying, Holland argued.
“I don’t have to work three jobs to feed my kids or pay my heating bills, which means that I can dedicate time towards fighting for the people that don’t have the means to fight right now and are being hit hardest,” Plummer said.
She went to St Mary’s Ascot, an expensive boarding school, and Tatler magazine, always attuned to its readers’ world view, headlined its story on the attack: “St Mary’s Ascot alumna charged with criminal damage for Van Gogh stunt.” Did Plummer laugh at that? “I did. Especially as I didn’t go to St Mary’s for very long. I went there for three years.”
Her involvement with Just Stop Oil began after she became frightened about the future and felt hopeless. “I’ve tried all the other things. I’ve gone on marches, I’ve signed petitions, I’ve written to MPs, I’ve made the individual lifestyle changes I feel like I can make.
“I’m vegan. I haven’t bought any first-hand clothes for four years, but it doesn’t make any meaningful change. We have to use these tactics now because we don’t have any time to waste. Our generation doesn’t have the luxury of sitting on the sidelines.”
She has lost one other luxury. Her bail conditions included that they cannot enter museums. “Shame,” Plummer said. “I do love art galleries.”
Soon, the judge’s warning suggests, it won’t just be museums that will be beyond the reach of Plummer and Holland. In the immediate aftermath of the National Gallery incident, Plummer claimed there had been, in addition to the criticism, an outpouring of support.
“A lot of people realise that this is a proportionate response to the criminality of the government,” she said of the soup throwing. “We’re scared little kids trying to fight for our future. What we did was not a criminal act. We’re not criminals.” Unfortunately for them, a court has now decided otherwise.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Just Stop Oil sentences will only strengthen resolve, jailed founder believes
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.subtitle: Roger Hallam says the jail terms handed out to activists could be a turning point that reinvigorates climate activism
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
The record jail sentences handed down to five Just Stop Oil activists could prove a “massive trigger event” for further action by the climate movement, Roger Hallam has said in an interview from prison.
Hallam, 58, was jailed for five years this month for orchestrating protests that disrupted the M25 over four days in November 2022 when 45 protesters climbed gantries on various parts of the motorway, forcing police to stop traffic.
Daniel Shaw, 38, Lucia Whittaker De Abreu, 35, Louise Lancaster, 58, and Cressida Gethin, 22, were each given four years after also being found guilty of conspiracy to cause a public nuisance.
The sentences handed down by Judge Christopher Hehir are thought to be the longest ever given for peaceful protest and have been widely criticised, with the United Nations human rights commissioner describing the measures as “deeply troubling” and “disproportionate”.
Speaking from a visiting room at HMP Wandsworth in southwest London, Hallam told The Times that the lengthy sentences had the potential to reinvigorate climate activism, which has struggled to recapture the same widespread intensity achieved in 2019 when Extinction Rebellion (XR) — which Hallam also co-founded — staged protests in central London for several weeks.
“It could be a massive tipping point, it could be a damp squib — it’s very difficult to predict,” he said. “The movement is at a fairly low point at the moment but it’s entirely possible that it will become massive again with a trigger event, not least people being put into prison for five years, and obviously the extreme climate events that are coming along the line.
“Insomuch as I’m a public figure, I’m a galvanising force for the movement and for the country to think about what it means to be vaguely sane and moral at this point when we’re about to destroy the biosphere.
“I think it’s very possible, or almost inevitable, that [the imprisonment of the five] will strengthen people’s resolve who already exist within the movement, and internationally as well.”
Just Stop Oil, in conjunction with XR and two other smaller groups, is planning to hold a protest outside parliament on Saturday, August 3, in response to the sentences, which insiders believe could attract the biggest turnout in years.
Detective Inspector Chris Rudd, who led the investigation into the five activists, said he feared their imprisonment may serve as a “rallying call” to other climate activists for a wave of protests.
Hallam has previously said “that if you’re not in prison, you’re not in resistance”, a view that other XR leaders disagreed with, precipitating his removal from the group’s strategic planning committee.
He went on to found the more radical Insulate Britain, which barricaded motorways with human roadblocks in late 2021, in the belief that the imprisonment of a smaller number of hardline activists would be a more effective way of forcing the government to act.
Just Stop Oil, of which Hallam is a leading member, has carried out a range of actions, from blockading oil terminals to throwing a tin of soup over Van Gogh’s Sunflowers.
Before founding XR, Hallam ran an organic vegetable farm in west Wales for 20 years. After his business began to fail following successive summers of heavy rain, he moved to London in 2015 to begin a PhD at King’s College studying civil disobedience methods.
The length of the sentence handed down to him was not surprising, he said, within the context of protest movements of the past.
“We have historical case studies of Martin Luther King and Gandhi and hundreds of other campaigns and what we are seeing broadly speaking is a classic backfiring effect when more extreme elements of the ruling class or opposition go overboard to try and do people in,” he said.
The legislative and judicial crackdown on protests in the UK in recent years comes at the same time that British prisons are grappling with huge overcrowding.
Describing the prison system as “the English gulag”, Hallam claimed that in the week he had been in Wandsworth, there had been two suicides and fights had broken out on a daily basis. For meals, he and other prisoners were fed boiled rice with fried rice one day, and boiled rice with pasta the next, he said.
He will use his time to record a podcast about the need for “spiritual grounding to create resilience in resistance”, a follow-up to a 12-part podcast called Designing the Revolution which he made while on remand for more than three months at Wandsworth in 2022.
He also intends to write a book about “the tragedy of modern conservatism”, which he says has failed to “realise that destroying the world for our future is a quintessential conservative concern”.
Before being imprisoned, Hallam had been working on a political project aimed at setting up citizens’ assemblies, which he believes will be the only way to deal with the many “ruptures” caused by climate change, such as starvation and mass migration, that he views as inevitable.
“The main problem at the moment is elites are demonstratively incapable of understanding their responsibilities and the objectivity of what we face,” he said, “and the judge in this case was an extreme but predictable example of that psychotic mindset.”

https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.subtitle: The actress and animal rights campaigner spoke out after Paul Watson, the founder of Sea Shepherd, was arrested in Greenland on a Japanese warrant
https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.text:
Brigitte Bardot, the 1960s French film star and animal rights activist, has criticised Japan over the arrest of a prominent Canadian anti-whaling activist.
France is pressing Denmark to release Paul Watson, 73, who was arrested in Greenland on a Japanese warrant on charges of wounding, damaging property and obstruction of business.
In an interview with Le Parisien, Bardot, 89, the former screen actress who has devoted her life to helping animals since the 1970s, said that âthe Japanese government â¦ launched a global manhuntâ against Watson which âcaught him in a trapâ. She added: âWe must do everything to save Paul.â
The detention of Watson, the founder of Sea Shepherd, a marine conservation campaign group, aboard his ship, the M/Y John Paul DeJoria, in the port of Nuuk on Sunday has prompted anger from environmentalists and celebrities in France. He once lived in the country and his muscular âdirect actionâ operations to obstruct whaling ships enjoy public support.
President Macron âis following the situation closely and France is intervening with the Danish authorities to ensure that Paul Watson is not extradited to Japanâ, the ElysÃ©e Palace said.
Macron was responding to an appeal by Sea Shepherd France, which said Watson had been illegally arrested by police who boarded his vessel on false pretences and led him to a van in handcuffs. Video of the episode has prompted anger among marine campaigners.
The activistâs ship had stopped in Greenland for fuel on its way to intercept a new Japanese whaling factory vessel in the north Pacific, according to the Captain Paul Watson Foundation (CPWF), his charity.
â¢ Pride and stubbornness behind Japanâs decision to resume commercial whaling
The police in Greenland, an autonomous Danish territory, said: âThe Japanese authorities have issued an international arrest warrant for Paul Watson, which is the reason why the Greenland police were ready to arrest him on arrival in Nuuk.â
The arrest was made based on a 2012 âred noticeâ from Interpol that circulated a Japanese warrant on charges of breaking into a Japanese vessel in the Antarctic Ocean in 2010, obstructing its business and causing injury as well as damage. The charges carry a potential prison sentence of more than five years.
A Danish court will review the case for extradition once Japan makes a formal request, the authorities said.
Watson, an advocate of direct action to halt whaling, sealing and other types of marine hunting, has been in scrapes with the law since he was dismissed in 1977 from the Greenpeace board of directors due to his opposition to their passive methods of protest.
His profile was raised internationally when he featured in the 2008 US television series Whale Wars, which showed his crews attempting to stop Japanese vessels killing whales off the coast of Antarctica.
Watson has been denied bail in Greenland because a judge deemed him a flight risk. He had fled house arrest in Germany in 2012 after he had been charged with offences stemming from his campaign against shark fishing. Local judges must decide by August 15 whether he should be extradited or released.
Watsonâs vessel, which has a crew of 25 volunteers, was due to sail through the Northwest Passage to confront the Kangei Maru, a new Japanese ship, as it makes its way southward in the Pacific. Its large capacity has fuelled suspicions that Japan is aiming to revive its whaling operations in the Antarctic Ocean.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Nine Just Stop Oil protesters arrested at Heathrow
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.subtitle: Activists detained near perimeter fence after promising a campaign of summer holiday disruption
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
Nine Just Stop Oil activists have been arrested at Heathrow during a summer “international uprising” by the environmental activist group.
The suspects were detained on Wednesday morning at two locations near the perimeter of the airport.
The Metropolitan Police said the activists were taken into custody on suspicion of conspiring to interfere with a site of key national infrastructure under the Public Order Act. Flights and other operations were not affected.
Video footage showed activists arriving on bicycles at a site close to passenger planes, outside a barbed wire fence, before an unmarked car pulled up and they were arrested.
A Just Stop Oil source told The Times last month that the group was planning a campaign to disrupt airports during the summer holidays as part of its drive to stop the use of fossil fuels by 2030.
Just Stop Oil said: “We refuse to die for fossil fuels. Continued burning of oil, gas and coal, as we pass irreversible tipping points that threaten to spin our climate out of control in a rapidly accelerating way, is jeopardising the stability on which our entire society depends.”
The group said the action was part of an “international uprising” and pointed to co-ordinated recent action taking place in other countries. This included affiliated activists blocking air traffic at Cologne Bonn airport in Germany, briefly suspending or diverting flights, and three people sitting next to the runway at Oslo airport for 30 minutes before being removed. Other incidents have taken place in Finland and Spain.
More than 1,000 lawyers, academics, artists and celebrities have criticised the “injustice” of sentences given last week to five members of the group who took part in a non-violent protest.
Roger Hallam, 58, was jailed for five years for co-ordinating the protest that disrupted the M25 over four days in 2022. Daniel Shaw, 38, Lucia Whittaker De Abreu, 35, Louise Lancaster, 58, and Cressida Gethin, 22, were each given four years in jail after being found guilty with Hallam of conspiracy to cause a public nuisance.
The Met said in a statement: “Nine Just Stop Oil activists have been arrested this morning for conspiring to disrupt Heathrow airport. Thanks to the work of officers involved, those arrested have been taken into custody and the Met has prevented significant disruption to the airport and travelling public.”
A spokesman for Heathrow said: “There has been absolutely no impact on operations whatsoever” and that “no one gained entry to anywhere they shouldn’t be”.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Minister backs record five-year jail term for Just Stop Oil founder
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.subtitle: Luke Pollard, the armed forces minister, welcomed the ‘strong message’ as Roger Hallam, was handed the longest sentence yet for non-violent protest
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
A five-year jail sentence for the founder of Just Stop Oil has been welcomed by a minister, who hoped it would send a “strong message” to other activists.
Luke Pollard, the armed forces minister, condemned the “pathetic” and “highly dangerous” behaviour of the direct action group for blocking roads. He claimed that the group had held up ambulances responding to emergency callouts, arguing it had sparked a public backlash and “set the case back” for tackling climate change.
Pollard told LBC radio: “I’m glad that there’s now been a strong message sent to them, and anyone thinking about that type of disruptive protest in the future, that there’ll be serious consequences if they go down that path.”
He added that the “strong penalties” imposed by a judge on five Just Stop Oil activists on Thursday were “welcome”.
Roger Hallam, 58, the founder of the group, ­received the longest ever jail sentence for non-violent protest under laws designed to crack down on public ­disruption. He was jailed for five years for co-ordinating the protests that disrupted the M25 in London over four days in 2022. Forty-five protesters climbed gantries on the motorway, forcing police to stop the traffic.
Daniel Shaw, 38, from Northampton, Lucia Whittaker De Abreu, 35, from Derby, Louise Lancaster, 58, from ­Cambridge, and Cressida Gethin, 22, from Hereford, were each sentenced to four years after being found guilty of conspiring to cause a public nuisance.
The sentences, handed down at Southwark crown court in London, were longer than those given to Just Stop Oil activists who scaled the Queen Elizabeth II Bridge over the Dartford Crossing in October 2022. They were condemned as a “gross miscarriage of justice” by environmental campaigners.
The group were sentenced under controversial legislation introduced by the previous government to get tougher on disruptive tactics used by ­environmental protesters, including blockading roads and attacks on sporting events. A 13-week campaign by Just Stop Oil (JSO) last summer cost the Metropolitan Police more than £7.7 million, the equivalent cost of 23,500 officer shifts.
The legislation, which provides for stiffer sentences for protesters who block roads, was backed by Sir Keir Starmer, now the prime minister. But it was condemned by the United Nations human rights commissioner as “deeply troubling” and “disproportionate”.
Prominent environmental campaigners, including the millionaire Labour donor Dale Vince and the broadcaster Chris Packham, criticised the sentencing of the so-called Whole Truth Five.
Speaking to The Times outside the court after sentencing, Vince, the founder of the electricity firm Ecotricity, said it “can’t be right” that protesters were jailed in the same week that it was announced prisoners would be released early to ease the prison crisis. He added that the sentence made the UK akin to “North Korea or Russia”.
When asked if Starmer should intervene, he said: “We have a government that understands the climate crisis and I do hope and believe they will intervene. I just think that in two weeks in power, there are bigger things occupying their mind.”
He continued: “This trial has been in process for a year. These are laws that were brought in by the Conservative government under Sunak and they are harsh and undemocratic.
“They make our country akin to North Korea or Russia, in terms of how we treat people that are dissident, that speak out and act out in their conscience. GBH and armed robbery, they are the kind of things you get five years for. I do hope they intervene because it is an injustice.”
Vince, a JSO backer who has donated almost £1.4 million to the Labour Party since 2014, including £710,000 in 2022, said that it was “ironic” that the protesters had been jailed for attempting to lobby the government to ban any new oil and gas contracts in the North Sea, a pledge that Labour plans to impose now it has formed a government.
The court was told that the M25 protests caused economic damage of £765,000, while the cost to the Metropolitan Police was more than £1.1 million.
The protests are also said to have ­affected more than 700,000 vehicles and left the M25 “compromised” for more than 120 hours.
Jocelyn Ledward KC, for the prosecution, told the court that the five ­defendants had joined a Zoom call in which they discussed the planned ­protests and were aiming to recruit others.
An undercover reporter for The Sun who joined the call pretending to be ­interested in the protest recorded part of the discussion and passed this to the police, who then ­arrested the activists.
In sentencing, Judge Christopher Hehir told the activists: “The plain fact is that each of you some time ago has crossed the line from concerned campaigner to fanatic. You have appointed yourselves as sole arbiters of what should be done about climate change.”
He told Hallam: “You are the theoretician, the ‘ideas’ man. In my judgment, you sit at the very highest level of the conspiracy.”
In a statement on his website Hallam said that the sentence was the work of a “kangaroo court”.
Hundreds of protesters gathered outside Southwark crown court to chant in support of the activists.
On two separate occasions, more than 100 people chased Serco prison vans they believed were taking the activists into court, with some attempting to block them by obstructing the road.
Some activists banged their palms against one van and shouted “we love you, Roger”, and others denounced the convictions as a “f***ing disgrace”. Police officers accompanying the van pushed the protesters away and formed a line to prevent them from following the vans further down the street.
In a press conference outside the court, campaigners spoke in support of the activists and decried the law as draconian.
Chris Packham, the naturalist and broadcaster, said the sentence was a threat to free speech and called for a meeting with Richard Hermer KC, the attorney-general, “as rapidly as possible” so that he could “address this grotesque miscarriage of justice”.
“Be clear, be very, very clear, this is not just about climate activism. The laws that have been drafted, the injustices that are being wrought, threaten all rights of free speech,” he said.
“We stand here today because our future security may be compromised by the reckless and irresponsible erosion of our human rights, of our fundamental freedoms.
“I stand here because I believe this represents the direct theft of our freedom, the destruction of our democracy, the deliberate and calculated intimidation of our protesters, and that, unless we resist this, the very real danger is our species will destroy life on Earth.”
• Tomiwa Owolade: These activists are posers, not persuaders
Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall, the celebrity chef and campaigner on food and environmental issues, said that protesters had been “really viciously sentenced under some extraordinary, wicked, malicious legislation”.
The sentence was also criticised by Tom Southerden, Amnesty International UK’s law and human rights adviser, who called on the Labour government to repeal the controversial policing act and protect the right to protest.
“These lengthy jail sentences for people seeking climate justice should increase the alarm over the ongoing crackdown against peaceful protest in this country, which violates all our human rights,” he said.
“With our overcrowded prison system already described as a ‘ticking time bomb’ by the new lord chancellor, these jail terms are all the more indefensible.”
The trial was criticised by Michel Forst, the UN’s special rapporteur for environmental defenders, who described the threat of a long sentence against Shaw as potentially unlawful. Speaking on the eve of the first day of the trial, Forst warned: “The ­imposition of such sanction is not only appalling but may also violate the United Kingdom’s obligations under international law.”
Roger Hallam, a 58-year-old farmer, founded Just Stop Oil and has since been described as the “spiritual leader” of the group.
Hallam’s activist journey began with organising rent strikes in London, before he co-founded the environmental action group Extinction Rebellion (XR) in 2018.
He has previously spent time in prison for his involvement in protests. In 2019 he was held in custody after being charged for his involvement in an XR plot to ground Heathrow traffic with drones but he avoided a jail sentence.
He was expelled from XR in 2019 when he was accused of downplaying the Holocaust for saying it was just “another f***ery in human history”. In the same year he claimed that the climate crisis would lead to “gang rape” in a pamphlet written while at Wormwood Scrubs prison.
After leaving XR he went on to found Insulate Britain, which carried out a series of road-blocking protests in the summer and autumn of 2021. The demonstrations, during which some activists glued themselves to motorways, led to the government tightening protest laws.
Daniel Shaw, who was accused of plotting the protest on the M25 with Hallam, is a 38-year-old social worker from Northampton.
He is described as softly spoken. He gained attention for his involvement in the sit-in at Kingsbury oil terminal in Warwickshire in September 2022.
He was among 51 protesters arrested for taking part in the lawful protest against new oil and gas projects in the UK. Six were later jailed.
Louise Lancaster, 58, is a former teacher from Cambridge and has been highly active in environmental protests.
The mother of three has been vocal about the urgent need for government action on climate change, criticising both the government and the media for their handling of environmental issues.
After the protest on the M25, she said: “The world is burning, it’s got to be obvious now to the people of this country, you have been lied to, fobbed off by the government and media fuelled by the oil barons and their greed.
“We have a serious emergency, action needs to be taken. The government must not license 40 new oilfields. The government must take swift action to stand by its climate pledges and protect the future for our young people.”
Cressida “Cressy” Gethin is a 22-year-old cellist from Herefordshire who was a music student at Cambridge. She was described by a JSO spokesman as an “impressively sharp and mild-mannered young woman”. Gethin was one of the protesters who scaled the gantry above the M25 near Heathrow in July 2022 to protest the UK reaching its hottest temperature on record, 40C, the day before.
She has been involved in other direct actions, such as a protest the same year in Grays, Essex, where she climbed on to pipework at an oil terminal to disrupt fuel storage and transportation. This act led to her being convicted for obstructing or disrupting legal activities, resulting in a 12-month conditional discharge and a fine.
She has faced legal consequences for her activism numerous times. She was found guilty of causing a public nuisance after the protest at Heathrow, which grounded numerous flights.
Lucia Whittaker De Abreu is a key activist who has played a significant role in several high-profile protests, including in the planning of the M25 motorway incident.
Whittaker De Abreu, 35, is from Derby. Her activism has led to numerous arrests and legal challenges. Her dedication to the cause has placed her at the forefront of the UK’s environmental protest movement.
Roger Hallam and four other environmental protesters were sentenced under beefed-up penalties brought in by parliament two years ago.
The Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022 was the first of two recent legislative moves designed to crack down on what the Conservative government and many others saw as increasingly disruptive tactics from environmental protesters.
The law gave senior police officers powers to impose conditions on protests, including setting start and finish times, and taking other measures that they deem necessary to prevent disorder. But only a year after that legislation received royal assent, the Tory government legislated again. What ultimately became the Public Order Act 2023 was referred to by detractors as the “anti-protest bill”. Its provisions included stiffer sentences for blocking roads and attracted the backing of Starmer.
The UN described the measure as “deeply troubling legislation”. Ministers dismissed its concerns and said that the fundamental right to protest was protected under the legislation.

https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.title: Spain announces first marine national park
https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.subtitle: The Canary island of El Hierro is set to become the site of a 24,000 hectare refuge for a rich variety of sea life, though some fear restrictions for tourism
https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.text:
The tiny Canary island of El Hierro is set to become the site for Spain’s first fully protected marine national park after years of lobbying by ecological groups.
The 24,000-hectare park will be established in the Mar de las Calmas, the sea off Restinga, Spain’s most southern settlement, which is an acclaimed diving sanctuary featuring coral gardens and inhabited by turtles, tuna, rays, dolphins, barracudas and the occasional whale shark.
“We have started the process that allows us to announce a new national park,” Teresa Ribera, the ecological transition minister, said. “The Mar de las Calmas is a unique place, perhaps the greatest in tropical and sub-tropical diversity. It will have the highest degree of protection.”
In an area close to the coast the seabed off El Hierro drops to 3,000 metres, providing habitats for a great wealth of species in a small space as well as rare species of algae. The area is prized by organisations such as Oceana, Greenpeace and the Spanish Institute of Oceanography.
Among the park’s supporters are the island’s traditional fishermen, who have continued their activity despite the establishment of a marine reserve in the area since 1996. But the old reserve covers only 750 hectares.
Michael Sealey, a senior policy adviser for Oceana Europe, one of the organisations behind the initiative, told El Diario news website: “The islanders have been very careful in the way they use marine resources. It is important to value this so that the islanders can continue their traditional activities as soon as the national park is implemented.”
The management of the maritime national park would be the responsibility of the central government, unlike in national parks on land. Among the groups that have opposed the park are sport fishing associations and some diving clubs, who are fearful that restrictions could increase.
Raúl Acosta Armas, a member of the regional parliament from the Agrupación Herreña Independiente party, which opposes the park, questioned the point of having a marine park off the island. He insisted on the importance of knowing “what prohibitions it entails”, saying that sport fishing or fishing for personal consumption “will be one of the limitations”.
Acosta also questioned the role that local administrations will play in running the park.
Natacha Aguilar, a researcher at the department of animal biology at the University of La Laguna, an expert on deep-water cetaceans and a native of El Hierro, told the state news agency EFE: “We must find the middle ground between taking advantage of the tourist attraction, the jobs that this can generate and not disturbing the tranquillity of the island, which is undoubtedly a special enclave with up to 18 species of cetaceans, four of them beaked whales, two of which are resident.”
Welcoming the park, Aguilar nevertheless warned that “everything could break down if the national park encourages uncontrolled tourism”, and advocated a tourist tax, limiting the number of visitors and tourist pleasure boats.
The proposal for the park will be open to four months of public scrutiny after which a draft law must be drawn up, which will have to be debated and approved in parliament, a process that may take several years.

https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/cele.text:
Good day, dearest Times reader, and welcome to the week when England fans all seem irrevocably glum after Sunday’s match — something I must admit I do not understand. We came second in the whole tournament. Second! Guys, surely that’s … really good? Out of 24 countries, we were one from the top! We got silver! Surely there cannot be any reaction to this other than a hearty “Hurrah!”?
I am, of course, aware that no one other than me is going “Hurrah!” right now but I genuinely don’t understand why. Comparing like for like, Britain is consistently either the sixth or seventh largest economy in the world, yet we don’t end every G7 summit with people crying in the streets because, once again, we didn’t beat the US to the top.
Ironically, in all the years the UK has been sliding down the World Happiness Report rankings — we’re at No 20 — everyone seemed quite chill about it. And yet now we come second in something that isn’t even money, or happiness, but achildren’s park game, andan entire country walks around as if it’s been burgled? I know I’m a vexingly bouncy optimist but I reallyfeel like we need to look on the bright side here. We’re turning football lemonade into lemons.
Obviously, I have now reached an age at which I don’t recognise the names of half the people mentioned in headlines. However, that really didn’t matter when I caught sight of the following news: “Peta Murgatroyd and Maks Chmerkovskiy reveal name of their newborn baby son.”
Ultimately, of course, none of us need to know who Peta Murgatroyd and Maks Chmerkovskiy are. All we need to do is hope that they gave little Murgatroyd-Chmerkovskiy Jr a first name that was both super short and easy to spell.
Since the invention of blue plaques — those classy azure lozenges alerting you to a house that was lived in by Dickens, briefly visited by Dickens or walked past by Dickens on the way to another blue plaque house he once sent a parcel to — their primary purpose has been to calmly celebrate the great and good. However, in recent years there has been an attempt to shake up who, and what, gets one — most pressingly with a continuing attempt to memorialise an infamous gig by the punk group the Clash that was held at the Corn Exchange, Bury St Edmunds, in 1978.
At the time, the gig — at which the Clash were supported by an early incarnation of the 2-tone legends the Specials — was accused of “causing mayhem … Punks were accused of damage to property, drunkenness, spitting and public urination.” Subsequently, certain types of live music, including punk, were banned in Bury St Edmunds for 20 years.
Those behind a local campaign for a blue plaque, headed by the punk fan Paul Johnson, 56, believe it is important to memorialise the gig: “There is a big void in Bury St Edmunds’ history because [after the Clash] established bands were not allowed here,” he told the BBC. “We could have had the good times but we were denied it. The council acted like they do in Footloose — they banned rock’n’roll.”
However, the Bury Society — a local historical group — are having none of it. “The Clash did not cover themselves with glory, during or after the event,” the group’s chairman Martyn Taylor, 73, said primly. “There’s a fine line you must draw between something that is accepted to moral standards and something that is not — and you must be careful how you tread that line. Is this something Bury wants to be remembered for?”
Well, let’s see what Bury is remembered for, blue plaque-wise. There’s one to memorialise a cellist who “bequeathed a fabulous collection of clocks to the people of Bury St Edmunds” and another to mark 100 years since the first Zeppelin air raid in Bury in 1916. With absolute inevitability, the Angel Hotel notes that Charles Dickens, author, once stayed there.
• My advice to the Conservative Party: guys, you’re hurt. Get drunk and lean into the hangover
Reading through these plaques I think I may have come up with a solution that will please Johnson and Taylor. If the Bury Society don’t want to mark the mayhem of the Clash gig, but Johnson wants to mark a bit of punk’s rebellious history, how about a plaque on the Bury Society’s offices reading “This is the building in which a blue plaque to commemorate the Clash’s controversial 1978 gig was declined”?
That way, Bury St Edmunds gets to remember the Clash’s uproarious gig, the Bury Society get to remind people that they like to walk a moral line, and everyone is satisfied. I’ll pop my $777,777 invoice in the post.
As he heads towards his 50th birthday, David Beckham is fulfilling the destiny of all men as they age: becoming low-down weird about something to the point of developing into a bit of an eccentric. In Beckham’s case, this eccentricity revolves around bees.
“Buzz off! David Beckham is accused of placing beehives on the boundary of his stunning £12 million Cotswolds country mansion to keep away nosy ramblers who peer over his fence,” ran the exhaustive headline in MailOnline.
After breathing into a paper bag, it continued: “Furious locals fear they could come under attack from swarming insects after the former England captain installed two new hives next to a public footpath.”
Of course we all knew Beckham was into bees: his much-publicised meeting with the King, in the spring, apparently revolved around discussions of each other’s beehives, and Beckham regularly gifts people jars of his honey, branded “DBee’z Sticky Stuff”.
This new development, however, suggests a slight shift in Beckham’s relationship with bees. To wit, he’s now invented guard bees? He’s got, like, a bee gang he hangs out with to protect him from other people? That’s some strong Cotswolds Mowgli shit.
This week it was suggested that Taylor Swift is not only the world’s most successful pop star, an icon to millions and a possibly pivotal figure in the forthcoming US election — “Taylor needs to back Biden again!” has been trending for some days now — but has also inadvertently made cheese more expensive too.
“Taylor Swift inflation lift in focus for the Bank of England,” one headline explained, suggesting that Swift’s seismic UK dates had caused a knock-on effect on inflation rates. Indeed, it’s not just the UK that’s been affected: so seriously is this being taken that the ECB’s Christine Lagarde has had to make a public statement clarifying “It’s not just Taylor Swift” that has kept eurozone inflation high. Millions of concert tickets, hotel rooms, friendship bracelets and last-minute purchases of pink cowboy boots on eBay are being blamed for a cut in interest rates becoming impossible.
There is one person, of course, for whom this theory will be incredibly welcome: Liz Truss. Still peeved at being blamed for Britain’s economic woes, the former prime minister has spent the past two years trying to assign liability to any and everybody else she can think of, in what I’m sure her aides refer to as “Operation Mad Arse-Save”.
And so now, as of this month, Truss’s “anti-growth coalition’’ — “Labour, the Lib Dems, the SNP, militant unions, vested interests dressed up as think tanks, talking heads, Brexit-deniers, Extinction Rebellion, podcasters, people who take taxis from north London townhouses to the BBC” — can now be joined by “the beloved pop icon and Shake it Off hit-maker Taylor Swift”.
I’m sure this will make Truss even more popular in the under-25 demographics the Conservatives are struggling to reach, and nothing bad can come of it! Go for it, Liz!
Well, we’ve now hit the point where we start rattling through all the different stages of summer at great speed. Glastonbury is done, Wimbledon is done, the Euros are done, localised flooding from unseasonal rainfall is done — and so we are officially into the next bit of the supposedly hot months: wedding season.
More specifically, A-list wedding season. If you are two people with a public profile and an urge to get some romantic paperwork done, then July and August are the peak months for having a wedding that will get the whole world talking. And what is the best way to get the whole world talking? Well, let me be brisk: it’s only two things. One: you throw insane amounts of money at it. And two: you invite as many pleasingly random celebrities as possible.
And so to “The Wedding of The Year” — the nuptials of Anant Ambani and Radhika Merchant, covered in every newspaper in the world. She is the heiress to a pharmaceuticals company, he is the son of the richest man in Asia, and their wedding has been estimated to cost more than $600 million (£460 million).
Just to put that into perspective, the London 2012 Olympics opening ceremony cost £27 million. Although, to be fair, Danny Boyle didn’t also have to pony up for a finger buffet or book a local covers band. He just got Kenneth Branagh to be Isambard Kingdom Brunel instead.
• The mystery of Stoke Park, a super wedding and Asia’s richest man
If you enjoy a random guest list — one that makes you go, “Huh? How do they know all these people? What life connects these guys?” — then you’ll enjoy the Ambani RSVP emails. The King and Queen of Bhutan, the rapper Akon, Bill Gates, the present and former prime minsters of Canada, Sweden and Qatar, Kim and Khloé Kardashian, Mark Zuckerberg, Justin Bieber, Ivanka Trump, Tony and Cherie Blair, Priyanka Chopra, Nick Jonas, star of Disney’s Camp Rock, Rihanna, the Backstreet Boys, and Boris and Carrie Johnson. Actually, it would be easier to say who wasn’t there because the full guest list was 14,000 people. Fourteen thousand! Try throwing your bridal bouquet into that! It’ll turn into the Battle of the Bastards!
Looking through the photos of the event we can see that, entirely predictably, Johnson turned out to be That Guy At A Wedding Who Didn’t Sort Out Childcare And Had To Bring His Kids. The three mini Johnsons were repeatedly snapped being carried around by their father in a room otherwise filled with adults drinking champagne who had notably not brought their children.
As we all know, a man at a wedding with a child will be perpetually on the lookout for some nice, sympathetic lady who can “just look after it for a minute while I pop to the lav?” And so it came to be that one of the most notable photos from the wedding was of Romy Johnson, 3, sitting on a sofa with Kim and Khloé Kardashian — both of whom already have an expression which reads, “That blonde guy has been gone for 45 minutes. What the f*** is going on?”
The date for the final ceremony — July 14 — was chosen for its astrological good fortunes. It is, of course, debatable just how much good luck you actually need when you’ve got $600 million to chuck at a wedding. After all, the catering isn’t dependent on whether or not, the night before the wedding, the father of the bride can rinse the middle of Lidl for half-price hot-dog buns.
Indeed, the couple’s pre-wedding gifts included a £62 million villa in Dubai, a £500,000 Bentley Continental and a £10 million diamond-and-pearl choker — plus a mega-yacht cruise on which the Backstreet Boys gave a private performance. At the wedding venue, one facility available to guests was an on-site pop-up antique shop. You could buy a 17th-century ormolu clock between speeches. At my wedding, our facilities weren’t far off: we had a Whack the Rat for the kids, made out of a piece of old drainpipe.
But, in a move I know might stretch your facilities, I’m going to ask you to, for a moment, be sympathetic towards the newly-wed Ambanis and their Wedding of the Year. Because imagine what a fuss it’s all been. Such a kerfuffle!
They had the first of three ceremonies in March, leaving a lot of time in between events to start fostering some panicky doubts about the whole thing. Imagine if you got “the ick” about your future husband the day before Tony Blair turns up on the back of an elephant. Or if you got cystitis on a yacht that also has Backstreet Boys on it singing at you. Every time you tried to get to the toilet, Nick Carter and AJ McLean would be dancing towards you in an arrow-head formation, and you’d just have to pretend you were getting a drink.
No, for those who have looked enviously at these pictures and thought, “I wish I had a dad who could spend over half a billion dollars on a wedding where the Kardashians ended up babysitting Boris Johnson’s kids”, I have to tell you: I think we’re all incredibly lucky we don’t.
Who wants to have the Wedding of the Year? Because you then have to embark on the Marriage of the Decade — and if any cracks show, even just one picture of you at a party together, looking peevish, you’ve got 14,000 guests all discussing it on WhatsApp, saying, “We flew all the way to an 18-acre business centre in Mumbai for this?”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Just Stop Oil activists spray Heathrow departure boards orange
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.subtitle: Two women arrested on suspicion of criminal damage
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
Climate activists have been arrested after spraying orange paint over departure boards at Heathrow Terminal 5.
Two Just Stop Oil (JSO) protesters staged a sit-in protest at the terminal, the home of British Airways, after spraying windows, floors and screens orange.
JSO said that Phoebe Plummer, 22, and Jane Touil, 58, were responsible for the protest, that they had entered the terminal at 8.35am and police had arrived within minutes to cordon off the area.
The two women were taken away to waiting police vans by 8.50am. The Metropolitan Police said two people had been arrested on suspicion of criminal damage and that officers remained at the scene to “deal with any further offences”.
Plummer was one of two activists found guilty last week of criminal damage after throwing tomato soup over Van Gogh’s Sunflowers in the National Gallery, and damaging its antique frame. Judge Christopher Hehir released Plummer along with Anna Holland, 22, on bail before sentencing on September 27. He told them to return to court “prepared in practical and emotional terms to go to prison on that date”.
Heathrow said that it was running as normal. A spokesman said: “Working with partners we have quickly resolved a protest incident in Terminal 5 and all involved have been removed from the airport.
“The airport continues to operate as normal and passengers are travelling as planned. We are in full agreement that the aviation industry needs to decarbonise, but unlawful and irresponsible protest activity is not the way forward and will not be tolerated.”
JSO issued a statement from Plummer after the Heathrow incident that said: “People around the world are rising up to demand an end to oil by 2030. This is an international problem, so ordinary people are doing what our politicians will not, working together globally to put a stop to the harm and suffering that fossil fuels cause.”
Twenty-four hours earlier, eight JSO activists were arrested at Gatwick. Seven of the group tried to block access to the south terminal’s central search area where passengers are screened. Video shared by the group showed passengers climbing over the protesters. The airport said that the group was quickly cordoned off and there was no disruption to departing passengers.
Last week, ten JSO activists suspected of planning to disrupt Heathrow were arrested. None of the activists was able to get into the airport, the Metropolitan Police said.
Climate activists have targeted airports around the world in recent days in a campaign named Oil Kills. JSO said that 21 groups across 12 countries have taken action at 18 airports so far.
Heathrow, Gatwick, London City, Stansted, Luton, Manchester, East Midlands, Leeds Bradford and Newcastle International airports have all won court injunctions against activists in recent weeks.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Ed Miliband criticises Just Stop Oil’s ‘disastrous’ tactics
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.subtitle: Energy secretary says climate activists are alienating people who care about environment in backlash against jail sentences for M25 protesters
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Just Stop Oil’s tactics are “disastrous” and have “alienated” those who care about environmental issues, Ed Miliband has said.
The energy security secretary said although he understood the motivation of the protest group, he could not back its methods because they were “driving people away” from moving to net zero.
Miliband would not be drawn on the jailing of five Just Stop Oil activists for protests on the M25. However, on JSO more generally he told Good Morning Britain on ITV: “I think their tactics are disastrous in terms of persuading people to come to our cause. Because when you saw what happened in relation to some of those protests — people not being able to go about their business, people not being able to get to see their relatives and so on — I don’t think that attracted people to the cause that I care about, it actually alienated them.
“So, my appeal to people who are thinking about these issues, who care passionately about these issue, is let’s see how we can build a coalition to support action of the kind that I’m talking about rather than driving people away from it.”
More than 1,200 artists, athletes and academics have condemned the “injustice” of the sentences given to the five JSO activists.
In a letter to Richard Hermer KC, the attorney-general, the writers backed the millionaire Labour donor, Dale Vince, and the broadcaster Chris Packham in their call for an urgent meeting to discuss “the jailing of truth tellers and their silencing in court”.
Roger Hallam, 58, was jailed for five years after being found guilty of conspiracy to cause a public nuisance for his involvement in a protest that disrupted the M25 outside London for more than four days in 2022.
Cressida Gethin, 22, Daniel Shaw, 38, Lucia Whittaker de Abreu, 35, and Louise Lancaster, 58, were each jailed for four years over the demonstration, in which 45 people climbed on to gantries over the motorway.
The jail terms are thought to be the longest sentences ever given for peaceful protest, and exceed those given to two JSO protesters for scaling the Queen Elizabeth II Bridge on the Dartford Crossing in October 2022.
Miliband said: “There has got to be upholding of the rule of law in this country and I as a politician am never going to get into second-guessing the decisions the courts make. This is a court case, a judge reached a decision, there may be appeals, so I’m not going to get into that.
“Let me say more generally, the right to peaceful protest is an important thing that this government values, including protests against us, and we have always got to look at the balance between that right to peaceful protest but also the severe disruption that can be caused to people, the severe damage that can be caused to people’s lives, people going about their everyday business.”
Sir Keir Starmer has faced calls to intervene in the case, and the UN human rights commissioner, Volker Turk, described the sentences as “deeply troubling”.
The artist Dame Tracey Emin, the Coldplay frontman Chris Martin, the film director Danny Boyle, the author Sir Philip Pullman, the singer Annie Lennox and the actor Toby Jones were among those who signed the open letter in support of Dale and Packham, who called last week for the meeting with the attorney-general.
Others who signed included the senior human rights lawyer Sir Geoffrey Bindman KC, the former Archbishop of Canterbury Rowan Williams and the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn.
They described the jail terms given to the activists, known as the Whole Truth Five, as “one of the greatest injustices in a British court in modern history”.
The letter said: “With prisons at breaking point and the new government acting urgently to address this, how can these sentences be seen as anything other than insanity? The sentences, ranging from four to five years, are higher than those given to many who commit serious sexual assault.
“The defendants were denied the right to explain to a jury why they took the action they did, making a mockery of the right to a fair trial, with the judge saying that the Crown Prosecution’s agreed facts on climate collapse — including that the world has gone beyond 1.5C for 12 consecutive months — were neither here nor there.”
The signatories argued that the non-violent protesters had been “fulfilling a necessary service by alerting the nation to the grave risk we all face, as scientists in their droves express their fear that many of the Earth’s systems are already at breaking point”.
During the trial at Southwark crown court, prosecutors alleged that the M25 protests had cost the economy at least £765,000, and the cost to the Metropolitan police was more than £1.1 million. The protesters also allegedly delayed more than 700,000 vehicles and “compromised” the motorway for more than 120 hours.
A spokesman for the attorney-general’s office said: “Decisions to prosecute, convict and sentence are, rightly, made independently of government by the Crown Prosecution Service, juries and judges respectively. The attorney-general has no power to intervene in these cases.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.title: Troon residents told to be on guard for Just Stop Oil during Open
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.subtitle: Police have called for vigilance as 200,000 fans descend on the Ayrshire town for the golf tournament
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.text:
Police have called on the residents of Troon to look out for criminal disruption and create a “network of vigilance” during the Open.
More than 200,000 golf fans are expected to descend on the Ayrshire town for the tournament which begins on Thursday. Specialist officers have urged those living and working in the community to become their eyes and ears during the event.
It is understood that they are particularly concerned about disruption being caused by members of Just Stop Oil. Members of the radical environmental group, which espouses non-violent direct action, brought last year’s tournament to a temporary halt when members coated a green with orange powder.
“The 152nd Open will be one of the biggest events Ayrshire has ever hosted,” said Chief Superintendent Alan Waddell. “It should be a historic occasion for the local community and golf fans across the world. We want everyone to be reassured by our visible presence and have the confidence to report anything that seems suspicious. Everyone has a part to play. We’ll have eyes and ears everywhere.”
A statement from the force added: “Specially trained Project Servator uniformed officers will be engaging with local businesses and those attending the event by handing out leaflets and explaining how people can play their part.”
A source close to preparations for policing big events told The Scottish Sun: “The Open is such a high-profile event with a real possibility of protest disruptions by groups like Extinction Rebellion or Just Stop Oil. There will be a large uniformed presence plus plainclothes officers mingling with the crowd so they can keep a close eye on things and react quickly if something was to happen.
“Police will have lots of intelligence and will know who the protesters are likely to be and what vehicles they are looking for. They will have people watching the motorways to keep tabs on who is travelling and there will be public order officers tucked out the way on standby just in case there is a large-scale containment required. But there will mostly be large numbers of community cops and, of course, spotters, like you get at football matches who know the ringleaders.”
If Just Stop Oil take action it would be the third consecutive year they would have targeted the Open. Last year Billy Horschel, the PGA Tour winner, was forced to intervene to prevent a group of activists from ruining proceedings further after they threw a smoke flare and orange power paint on the 17th green at the Royal Liverpool. At the event Martin Slumbers, R&A chief, revealed that a prior attempt at hitting the tournament had been stopped a year before.
Referring to the 2022 Open, which took place at St Andrews, he said: “There was direct intelligence last year, and most people in this room don’t know that the Open was targeted last year. We have significant security procedures in place. We work clearly with the law enforcement agencies, and we’ll wait and see what happens.”
Other high-profile events targeted by the group include last year’s Wimbledon and World Snooker Championship and the Ashes Test at Lords.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Extinction Rebellion plans mass occupation of Windsor Castle grounds
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.subtitle: The group invited the King and ‘all people of good hearts and good conscience’ to join them for the three-day protest action in Windsor Great Park
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
Thousands of Extinction Rebellion protesters will stage a mass occupation of Windsor Great Park in a direct challenge to the King for three days next month.
The occupation will take place from August 30 until September 1 in the grounds of Windsor Castle in Berkshire, XR announced.
Quoting Harmony, a book the King wrote while still the Prince of Wales, the protest group said Charles “clearly understands the plight of the planet and the urgent need for society to change course”.
The group acknowledged that the King is expected to be less vocal about climate change and environmental destruction now that he is the reigning monarch as it is seen as “too political”.
Although they insisted the occupation will not be targeting a person but “the system”, XR invited the King “and all people of good hearts and good conscience” to join them for “three days of beauty, community, action and democracy”.
“The occupation will unite everyday people fighting for climate justice, global justice, social justice, and justice for nature, to demand an upgrade to our democratic system,” the group said.
The purpose of the “peaceful event” is to advance the group’s demand that the government must create and be led by a citizen’s assembly on climate and ecological justice.
Catherine Bartlett of Extinction Rebellion UK said: “Windsor Castle has been chosen as an embodiment of a broken and unjust system where our message will resonate powerfully. The general election has neither fixed our broken system nor addressed the urgent action needed to tackle the climate and nature emergency.”
“Aristocrats, oligarchs and corporate interests have infected and distorted our politics and media for their own benefit and at our expense. Our politics is failing us from top to bottom. It’s time for a democratic upgrade. We demand better at all levels; from the head of state to local councils but our central demand is for a citizens’ assembly on climate and ecological justice, which is needed more urgently now than ever before.”
The group wrote to the King on June 13, informing him of their plans and requesting he do all he can to help facilitate the protest.
In the letter the group said: “On the weekend of August 30 to September 1 we will bring thousands to your door in Windsor to protest at the failure of our government to act on the science of climate change and ecological collapse.
“We refuse to bequeath a dying planet to future generations by failing to act now. We act in peace, with ferocious love of these lands in our hearts. We act on behalf of life.”
Buckingham Palace has been approached for comment.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Water companies told to clean up or face special measures
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.subtitle: Steve Reed, the new environment secretary, has said cleaning up Britain’s rivers, lakes and seas is one of his five core priorities
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
Water companies will have no choice but to clean up their act under the new government, 10 Downing Street has said.
Sir Keir Starmer’s spokesman was unwilling to be drawn on what would happen if Thames Water, which will release its full-year financial results on Tuesday, collapses under huge debts and shareholders’ reluctance to invest.
“I’m not going to get ahead of that. The government has said in its manifesto that it will put failing water companies into special measures so they have no choice but to clean up their act,” the spokesman said.
This week is crunch time for the water industry’s hopes of investing £100 billion on new infrastructure, to clean up Britain’s polluted waterways. On Thursday, Ofwat will decide how much of the sum can be spent over the next five years. The regulator is expected to trim the total investment to protect households from water bill rises of up to 73 per cent in some regions.
“We’ve clearly seen an unacceptable situation where not enough has been done by the sector to tackle the issues around pollution,” said the prime minister’s spokesman. Wet weather last year saw raw sewage spills double in duration to the highest level on record.
Steve Reed, the new environment secretary, said in a video released on Monday: “It will take years to reverse the damage that has been done.” He said that cleaning up Britain’s rivers, lakes and seas was the first of his five core priorities, which also include food security and restoring nature.
Among the tasks in Reed’s in-tray is working out what the trigger should be for banning bonuses for polluting water companies, a flagship Labour manifesto pledge. Water company bosses have taken £26 million in bonuses and long-term incentives since the 2019 election, one analysis found.
The previous government had copied the bonus ban policy and instructed Ofwat to look into implementing it, but no criteria had been set out, such as breaching an annual number of pollution incidents classified by the Environment Agency as serious.
On average, water companies will raise household water bills 33 per cent by 2030 to £585, if Ofwat this week gives a green light to the full £100 billion that firms want to spend.
However, campaigners and celebrities have urged the government to pause the regulator’s decision, which has already been postponed by the election. Stephen Fry, the actor, Joe Lycett, the comedian, Michael Rosen, the author, and a group of activists said: “We are asking you to pause the current price setting process and start a root-and-branch public review of ownership and regulation immediately.”
The group, which includes campaigners from around the country, plus unions and charities including Greenpeace and River Action, said: “The public and our rivers and seas must not be asked to bailout failing shareholders, through higher bills, lower standards, or state-restructuring.”
Separately, researchers said that they had found fibreglass in shellfish in the south of England. A study by a team across Brighton, Portsmouth and Southampton universities found evidence of the fibres in oysters collected in Chichester Harbour. “I don’t want to venture and predict what would be the effect on the human body, but I think the ‘asbestos-like fibres’ should be quite a warning,” said Dr Corina Ciocan, principal lecturer in marine biology at the University of Brighton.
The Times is demanding faster action to improve the country’s waterways. Find out more about the Clean It Up campaign.

https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.title: Miliband’s North Sea raid will send a £20bn bill taxpayers’ way
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.text:
Since Shell tried to scuttle an oil storage buoy off the west coast of Scotland in 1995, energy companies have had to dispose of offshore installations on dry land when they’re decommissioned.
Shell’s plan to sink the redundant Brent Spar caused outrage on environmental grounds. Greenpeace activists boarded it from a helicopter and drivers boycotted Shell petrol stations. Forced into a U-turn, Shell towed Brent Spar to a Norwegian fjord, where it was dismantled at almost ten times the cost. Three years later, governments of the northeast Atlantic region agreed to ban the at-sea burial of installations for good.
Under rules dating back to 1975, taxpayers pick up roughly half the cost of scrapping offshore structures when they go to the big oil field in the sky. The forecast decommissioning cost for the entire North Sea moves around depending on levels of activity and efficiency gains, but it stood at £40 billion last year, according to the government-owned North Sea Transition Authority. The exchequer will be on the hook for about £20 billion in the form of relief on operators’ past and future taxes.
That bill will start arriving a decade sooner than it might have done if Ed Miliband, the new energy secretary, goes ahead with his promise to soak the North Sea oil and gas industry.
Labour’s manifesto vowed to increase the Conservatives’ windfall tax on profits, bringing the total to 78 per cent; take away “unjustifiably generous investment allowances”; and stop issuing licences for new exploration. It said the extra windfall tax would reap £1.2 billion a year, or £6 billion over this parliament, which would go towards funding state-owned GB Energy.
The North Sea had two booms, in the mid-80s and the late-90s. It has gushed net tax revenues of more than £300 billion and in its heyday accounted for more than 10 per cent of all government receipts. It has been in decline for years, but accelerating that would be economically and environmentally illiterate.
Contrary to perceptions, “majors” such as Shell and BP make up just 30 per cent of North Sea output. Most sites are now owned by smaller quoted companies such as Harbour, Ithaca and Serica. Hitting them with higher tax and withdrawing investment allowances would result in production and job cuts, most of them in Scotland. Analysts at Stifel say Labour’s extra windfall tax would raise a maximum of £5 billion because it would force the sector into “rapid decline”. After an initial spurt, it would result in a lower tax take.
Choking off domestic supply of oil and gas while it is still in demand would simply offshore emissions. The best argument is a flimsy one — that it would give the UK greater moral clout to urge other countries towards net zero and add to the ostracisation of fossil fuels.
The above is fairly well-trodden ground. Less fully explored has been the impact that the North Sea’s premature demise would have in terms of decommissioning costs. Stifel reckons Labour’s plans would shift the pattern of payments forward by about ten years, with a big spike in the early 2030s. It says that from about 2040, the government would be paying more to the oil and gas industry in tax relief than it received in revenues — as it did in 2016-17, when falling commodity prices made the North Sea a net drain for the first time.
In an era when chancellors scrabble around for single-digit billions of “headroom” in fiscal forecasts, the advancing of a £20 billion outlay matters. There is also what PR people would call “optics”. If Labour wins a second term, is it going to be happy seeing billions of pounds flow out to evil oil and gas companies? Consider that in light of former justice secretary Alex Chalk’s comment last week that in straitened times, new prisons had to be weighed against new hospitals.
There would be a temptation to renege on the payments. That’s where the industry and the last government saw this one coming. In 2013, to give North Sea operators confidence that the decommissioning regime wouldn’t change in the future, Sajid Javid as economic secretary to the Treasury announced a new arrangement. The government would enter into legally binding deeds with oil and gas companies guaranteeing them decommissioning tax relief at 2013 levels in perpetuity. Within five years, the Treasury had signed more than 80 deeds, according to the National Audit Office. A deed has been called on at least once: in 2017-18, the Treasury paid £45 million to one operator and set aside a further £299 million for future years.
An oil and gas veteran says any government attempt to cancel these deeds would be “horrible”. But the companies would probably win in court.
To be fair, all this was a known fly in the oil barrel. Miliband is only doing what he said he’d do in opposition. I backed Labour at this election because the Tories needed to go. I could swallow this fly — and another, Labour’s workers’ rights package — for the greater good.
But it is worth thinking about — not just because of the implications for taxpayers but because it prefigures inevitable tensions to come between idealists such as Miliband and realists such as chancellor Rachel Reeves. We must hope the latter camp wins out.
To end on a more positive note, Sir Keir Starmer has made some excellent external appointments — notably Sir Patrick Vallance as science minister and James Timpson on prisons. Varun Chandra, boss of intelligence firm Hakluyt, is thought to be set for a business role. Sir Nigel Wilson, the former Legal & General chief, would be helpful on housing. It’s reminiscent of Gordon Brown’s “government of all the talents”, known as the “goats”.
