https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Saintly quest of eco-zealot will lead more astray
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
Those who set themselves up for sainthood ought to be judged by harsher standards than the rest of us. In the case of the Extinction Rebellion co-founder Roger Hallam, sentenced last week to five years in prison after his involvement in a conspiracy to shut down one of our busier motorways, two standards can be applied.
To what extent is Hallam motivated by personal vanity — by a sense of himself as a bruised, flinty, oracular man with a ponytail telling British society hard truths; such hard truths, in fact, that its only response is not to listen to them but to bang him up in prison?
Second, do Hallam’s positions — that a global carbon elite is planning to kill billions of people, that western political “regimes” will be swept away within ten years after revolutionary action, and so on — represent a significant, even mainstream current of thought in Britain?
• Extinction Rebellion plans mass occupation of Windsor Castle grounds
On the vanity count, the verdict is surely in. Hallam suffers from a full-blown sainthood complex, a desire to be the British Gandhi. You might forgive him his (sadly accurate) self-description during his latest trial that he is the “most influential environmentalist in the country apart from David Attenborough”.
But other claims made by Hallam down the years are less persuasive and hint at a peculiar egotism. He once compared Extinction Rebellion to the White Rose movement. The latter were students who protested against the Nazis inside Germany during the Second World War. Some of its members were beheaded.
Climate protesters like Hallam usually receive fines and small custodial sentences, not one-way trips to the guillotine presided over by jackbooted Nazis. Hallam is always loud-mouthing like this. His public statements are intensely preoccupied with Nazis, gas chambers, gang rape and genocide. These will all become part of our lives, Hallam argues, should his climate activism fail. It must be a heroic burden to shoulder.
There is also the extraordinary account he gives of his own life story. Hallam tells us his path was decided at the age of 13. He began obsessing over the “question of political effectiveness”, he wrote in a 2019 letter called “Advice to Young People, as You Face Annihilation”. How, he wondered, could politics make the world a better place?
From this early age, Hallam says he never changed. Yes, he worked for a while as an organic farmer, and yes, he tells us an academic at King’s College, London, told him that he was the “best PhD student he had ever supervised” while he studied there. But Hallam says he never stopped thinking about the “question of political effectiveness” from the moment he hit puberty.
Even Gandhi, who transformed from a top hat-wearing lawyer in South Africa to a half-naked spiritual leader in the Raj, underwent a kind of personal development. Hallam tells us that he knew society was sick, sought out the means to transform it, and never second-guessed this insight.
This is a straightforward, revealing admission of authentic long-range fanaticism. It’s also the crude heart of his appeal. If you never change you are unlikely to become a hypocrite.
• The Times view on criminal protests: Just Stop Offending
How wide is that appeal? Christopher Hehir, the judge who sentenced Hallam at Southwark crown court last week, described him as a “fanatic” who, along with four other defendants, had appointed themselves the “sole arbiters of what should be done about climate change, bound neither by the principles of democracy nor the rule of law”.
Yet Hehir was forced to admit something else as he sent the group to prison: “I acknowledge that at least some of the concerns motivating you are,” he said, referring to the scientific and social consensus around the hard fact of climate breakdown, “at least to some extent, shared by many.”
It’s worth teasing out what those concerns are. Within our lifetimes, and certainly within our children’s, Hallam and his followers believe we will end up in a reality no different from Cormac McCarthy’s 2006 novel The Road. Social collapse, roving bands of killers, human life reduced to the nasty, brutish and poor factory setting of pre-civilisational Homo sapiens.
In Britain these are no longer eccentric concerns. Thousands and thousands of people believe that The Road reality is coming at us, fast. At the Restore Nature Now rally last month, a much bigger political gathering than anything the mainstream parties could muster during the general election, this doom mood was everywhere.
Sure, there were men walking around central London with flowerpots on their heads and smiling women dressed up as bees. But whenever I spoke to marchers, the conversation usually drifted towards Hallam-esque places.
British environmentalists, the sort who are members of the RSPB and have family recipes for lemon drizzle cake, genuinely think their children may end up being eaten by cannibal gangs unless we build more onshore wind turbines and ban cheap short-haul European flights.
“When the shit hits the fan, I’ll be dead,” one 68-year-old retiree told me, before warning that maize will be the first crop to die out and plunge us into food riots. A bloke who taught “slow yoga” told me western societies were too driven and brutal, before cheerfully explaining why we needed a new Guy Fawkes to “give parliament a shake up”.
When Roger Hallam was a 13-year-old fantasising about social and political change, these were fringe positions. They no longer are. Surveys repeatedly show that the majority of British adults “worry” about climate change.
At Restore Nature Now, attended by about 60,000 people, including celebrities like Chris Packham and Dame Judi Dench, those worries were expressed: not only that dolphins, whales and barn owls were dying out. The worry is bigger — that life as we know it will soon completely change for the worse. This is a genteel British apocalypticism, the soft underbelly of the more extreme views that have helped to put Hallam in prison.
At the moment, most of this feeling is being mopped up by the Green Party, with their four new MPs and expanding roster of local councillors. It may not be contained there for too long. The Greens won almost 7 per cent of the vote at the general election, which translated to 0.6 per cent of MPs. Without equitable representation, it does not take much imagination to see how some of those voters will end up on their own Hallam-like quests for sainthood.

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Vandalism, theft, risking lives. I think that makes Mr Just Stop Oil a career criminal
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
What would you say defines a cult leader? Charisma, prolixity, mania — many of them have these distinct, unsettling qualities. If you look at any extremist, though — any political headbanger, any messiah-like ruler — there’s one thing they all have. A complete, psychotic inability to understand what it is like to be another person, or even care. They may preach good for society, but they don’t take any interest in it, or even understand what it is. It is why they often prefer animals.
Take, for example, the Just Stop Oil convicts. How can they be so appalling?
Five of them were arrested in October; they’ve now been given huge sentences. One, Roger Hallam — a thin, grey, unlaundered man, half badger, half High Sparrow — was handed five years, for telling people to clamber up onto M25 gantries. I don’t need to tell you how dangerous this is — it is even more dangerous than blocking ambulances on blue lights, cancer patients, sick children etc, which Just Stop Oil protesters also did. Others ran out onto the motorway in dark, wet, winter conditions — it is amazing no one died.
But it’s not ever us, obviously, who are the victims; it is always — always — them.
Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall, of all hilarious, carrot-adjacent people, decided to defend Hallam outside court, saying every citizen had a right to engage in “peaceful protest”. A columnist, George Monbiot, thundered that one of them wasn’t even at the M25: he’d been simply found guilty of organising the protest, “merely appearing on a Zoom call”. Is that an excuse he’d extend to a terrorist? Hmm, on second thoughts I expect he would.
Chris Packham, meanwhile, demanded time with the new attorney-general; the heavy sentences were an assault on “free speech”. It’s funny, but I’d always put him more in the “words are violence” camp than in the “I can cope with your arguments” camp. Who cares, though, when there’s a narrative to abuse and manipulate?
I’m not, by the way, someone who minds protest — it’s all good copy. The more you take away people’s right to freedom of expression, the further we drift towards a flavourlessness, a dangerously passive society.
But you can’t argue it is “peaceful protest” if you put people in danger or run the risk of dying yourself. It’s like being five years old, throwing a stone and then arguing later it was fine because it didn’t hit anybody. To ignore this, to pretend it doesn’t exist — to totally overlook the feelings/safety of your fellow citizens — shows a chilling, almost psychotic disregard for what holds us together as a society.
It’s very now, though, this humourless, dogmatic, sterile approach to politics.
Read Hallam’s blog and you will be beckoned into a bleak, sociopathic, me-me-me netherworld.Almost no one lives up to his expectations; certainly not liberals, nor even the left, which he thinks is made up of “dumb” people who “make me want to throw myself off a cliff”. The only politician he appears to like is one anonymous Tory MP, who, on hearing — I’m just guessing — about his love of the earth, rolling hills and the purity of nature, declared him a “true conservative”. Well, that’s what they said about the similarly eco-obsessed fascist leader Mussolini, isn’t it?
Most of Hallam’s stunts are charmless, by the way: defacing property; shoplifting food “to highlight the instability of global food distribution”. How does stealing do that? If he weren’t old and middle class with a PhD in — yes — “civil disobedience”, you would describe him as a career criminal.
Who does he think he’ll convert? By harassing, provoking and inconveniencing the ordinary citizen, climate protest has changed, vastly, in the past few years. It has gone, like most things, from wild, passionate and creative to nihilistic, dark and cannibalistic. The target is not corporations but “sheeple” — protest by shaming insult. Why attack the people you’re meant to be persuading, though?
But that is to misunderstand the mindset. We live in a world where only “my” thoughts, fears, worries and opinions matter: my misanthropy. It’s the height of individualism. You get to a point where people are so self-obsessed they won’t accept anything, not even a lawyer. As one police officer pointed out, most Just Stop Oilers now “self-represent”.
Law, of course, is the single most important cultural unifier. It is the product of centuries and centuries of common ground, decided by reasoned thinking. You can attack this law or that for being passed by “New Labour” or “the Tories” (I’m sure Hallam would say both), but without it society falls apart.
To show contempt for the law is what serial killers and sociopaths do; they are people who refuse to face their sentences. Hallam and his fellow control freaks take things even further, though: they screamed, they shouted, they talked over the judge; were rearrested, in court, nine times — three times alone for Hallam. You just think: who are these animals?
Hallam will no doubt argue it is unacceptable that he gets a large sentence when petty criminals, for example two asylum seekers who stole a man’s £25,000 Rolex, “walk free”. I don’t agree. He is an organiser, the head of the snake: he threatens large numbers of people; the greater the misery, the happier he is. Getting arrested, burdening the system, slowing things down: it’s his aim. We will spend over a quarter of a million pounds imprisoning him — a lot for one man’s vanity project.
As for the police, they will oppose harsh sentences, seeing them as a “rallying cry” to other activists. Barely a protest has gone past without the police letting Just Stop Oil activists trample all over them, though, so why wouldn’t they continue the trend?
Keir Starmer should ignore pleas for leniency. Remember it’s the same people who attacked Stonehenge — I have never seen him so angry. “Pathetic,” he tweeted.
Dink dongk! Vat’s zat noise? Ja, it is ze doorbell rinkingk.
And who is at the door?
It is I, your German nudist pen pal from 2001, Klaus — the one who, even after 23 years, won’t stop writing. I am here! Hallo!
This, dear reader, is my way — and pisstakers on the internet’s way — of spiriting you into the incomparable new Loewe ads, in which Daniel Craig — James Bond — is trussed up in leather, boots and chunky Deutschland 83 knits, like an unflushable Tyrolean exchange student. There’s a set of incredible pics, including one with green, mollusc glasses and a straightened swoop of pond-scum forelock. It’s a fashion car crash.
Why do celebs do this?
According to a fashion editor friend, it is Craig’s equivalent of Trussonomics. A quite straight, uptight brand, he’s suddenly betting the farm on some weird look. The vibe is, says the fashion editor, “somebody stop her. It reeks of Y2K disposable camera. Also: the return of Babyliss hair straighteners.”
As for Loewe, I can’t even begin to imagine how thrilled this ho-hum Spanish luxury goods house must be, having nabbed 007 and crammed him into its frankly ugly gear, only to see a massive viral hit. As they say in Spain, long live Craig’s tortured outbursts.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Mum got four years for renting a safehouse for Just Stop Oil
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.subtitle: The family of Louise Lancaster, who was sentenced this month for her role in the M25 protests, say they are shocked at the punishment but back her fight against climate change
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
As a young woman, few things worried Louise Lancaster more than the idea of letting people down or doing something embarrassing. Having been one of the co-organisers of the protest that reduced parts of the M25 to gridlock over four days in November 2022, it seems that in later life she managed to overcome those challenges.
“For the woman I married to become the woman she is now, she’s had to go against the principles she was raised with,” says her former husband Tim Lancaster. “To get to the stage where she could face off a police officer and risk arrest … all of that was hard for her. Really hard. The fact she was going to inconvenience people was the most difficult part. She wouldn’t have done it if she’d been able to see another way.”
Together for 28 years until their amicable split last year, Tim, 57, who worked in IT, and Louise, 58, a special educational needs co-ordinator before her retirement two years ago, became involved in climate change activism in 2019. They joined marches, signed petitions and wrote to their local MP.
“For a while we thought people were noticing,” Tim says. “But Lou said to me, ‘Look, we did all of that and nothing changed — we have to do something else.’ Around 2020 she started to see non-violent direct action as a way of getting the government’s attention. “Lou studied maths at Oxford. She looks at data and she works things out. She thought about it very carefully.”
Handing down record sentences for non-violent protest earlier this month, Judge Christopher Hehir told the court that Louise and her co-conspirators, Roger Hallam, 58, Daniel Shaw, 38, Lucia Whittaker De Abreu, 35, and Cressida Gethin, 22, had “some time ago … crossed the line from concerned campaigner to fanatic” before they attended a Zoom meeting in which they planned to recruit 45 volunteers to climb gantries over the M25.
The judge described the protest as causing “massive disruption”, including missed exams, funerals and cancer appointments. It allegedly cost the Met Police £1.1m and impacted around 700,000 vehicles, leaving the motorway “compromised” for more than 120 hours. Lancaster did not herself take part, but she had climbed a gantry on the M25 in an earlier protest in July 2022.
On the Zoom call, Hallam, the co-founder of Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion, said that they intended to cause “the biggest disruption in British modern history” in an effort to force the government to meet one of Just Stop Oil’s core demands: an end to new oil and gas exploration in the North Sea.
In a decision that has provoked fierce debate, Hallam was jailed for five years for compromising to cause a public nuisance, while Louise, who paid more than £1,000 to rent the Airbnb where protesters stayed, and also bought climbing equipment, was sentenced to four, along with Shaw, Whittaker De Abreu and Gethin.
With Tim on our video call on Thursday night are the couple’s three grown-up children. Tristan, 27, is a software engineer; Verity, 25, is a midwife; and Theo, 19, is a medical student. They are bunched together, legs dangling off the edge of a single bed in the family home in the village of Grantchester, near Cambridge. Tim and Louise divorced in November but remain good friends.
“Whenever I think of my mum I think: unrelentingly kind,” Theo says. “In almost any situation she will put others first.”
Tristan, Theo and Tim visited Louise in Bronzefield, a female prison that houses category-A prisoners in Surrey, on Monday afternoon. “I’d had an interview for a summer job and the first thing she asked was, ‘How did it go?’” Theo says. “With me being the youngest, she has always been very open about what might happen and took into account my thoughts. She cares about us — if we’d said, ‘Mum, don’t do it,’ she wouldn’t have taken part.”
Verity visited the previous Tuesday, two days before the sentencing on July 18, along with Louise’s worried elderly father, a retired art teacher with whom, Tim says, she has had some pretty fiery exchanges. “He said he felt her activism has ‘let the family down’.”
“I gave her a hug and then burst into tears,” Verity says. “Mum broke into a massive smile and said, ‘I’m going to be fine.’ She told me she’d been helping other women filling out forms and she was going to do some online courses and work on her pull-ups.” Her brothers fall about laughing at this. “It’s very not-Mum.”
“She expected that this might happen,” Tim explains, “and she prepared herself and everyone else for it.” Nonetheless the family was shocked at the length of the sentence. “To get a sentence that is way longer than you’d get for violent crime [the average UK sentence for violent crime is 21.6 months]. It feels terribly unjust.” The Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022 allows such harsher punishments to be imposed.
Under the Public Order Act 2023, provisions also came into effect earlier this year that give the police more power to clamp down on disruptive protests. Did they not wish that Louise had done something else? Lobbying parliament perhaps? Or chaining herself to railings? “She has — and it hasn’t been enough,” Tristan insists. “Big Oil has known for decades that burning fossil fuels is dangerous but has carried on regardless, and successive governments have done nothing to stop it.”
The family is not sure if there will be an appeal against the sentences, but so far a crowdfunder has raised £60,000 to pay for legal fees. The cost would be hundreds of thousands of pounds. Instead they are pinning their hopes on the new government looking at the law. “I never thought as an Englishman I’d ever see rules as draconian as this in my country,” Tim says. “But Lou is resigned to doing her time.”
Louise was initially struggled to get any vegan protein or exercise in prison. But speaking to her on Friday, Tim reported back that she had at last received some suitable food.
In the course of her activism, Louise has incurred fines of more than £20,000, which she will struggle to pay off. She’s been strip-searched, handcuffed face-down and the house has been raided more than once by police. The emotional cost to the family is high. “Johnny and I are getting married next summer, Mum’s gutted to miss it. Maybe she’ll get out with a tag and she can wear a long dress,” Verity says, a little too brightly.
Tim describes Louise as a sensitive soul, someone who “listens more than she speaks”. Could Louise be in so deep she can’t see the wood for the trees? Verity says not. “She knew what she was putting people through. And it was a big moral dilemma. Her position was that there is a much bigger disaster at stake — if we don’t act quickly — than people being late for school and work.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.title: Labour MPs must start fighting for Scotland — and soon
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.text:
Catching up with some of the new Scottish Labour MPs in Westminster watering holes last week, the mood could perhaps be summed up as comfortably numb. They’re pleased, of course, deliriously so in many cases. But like people who have just won the lottery, they’re not entirely sure what to do with their good fortune and a little anxious that they might not deserve it.
This is not a bad thing. Politicians should be anxious to do well and not take their success for granted. They desperately need to avoid triumphalism and gloating, especially in the hearing of hacks like me. Margaret Thatcher’s deputy, Willie Whitelaw, famously remarked after a Labour setback: “Wrong to gloat. Mustn’t do it, no, no, no. But I can tell you inside I’m gloating like hell.” That goes for Labour and the SNP.
I bumped into the new Na h-Eileanan an Iar (Western Isles) MP, Torcuil Crichton, already being described as “Westminster’s coolest MP”. He said he didn’t realise his 23 per cent swing from the SNP was the biggest in Scotland. Maybe the former political editor of the Daily Record had diplomatic amnesia. But the absence of gloat was admirable.
Once they’ve got over the initial shock of victory, this formidable phalanx of 37 Scottish Labour MPs must make sure they don’t sink into irrelevance — rather as the SNP’s even larger contingent of MPs succeeded in doing. The “Fighting 56” passed through Westminster largely without trace. The 37 “Starmtroopers” could go the same way.
Independence isn’t coming back soon, so the task of the Scottish Labour group might seem easier to the extent that the constitutional issue is resolved for the time being. Labour can forget about demands for repeat referendums, legal challenges and the Yes campaign stealing their activists.
The Union may be safe, but that isn’t job done. Labour MPs must remember that they’re representing Scotland, which remains a nation in its own right albeit as part of the UK, with its own culture, economy and interests. They have to be seen fighting Scotland’s corner. Above all, they have to avoid defaulting back into the “branch office” syndrome.
They need to be bolshier and more awkward than the Nats. There was a curious lack of bolshy from The 56. They always seemed to be waiting orders from “Stalin’s wee sister”, as Jim Sillars rather unfairly called Nicola Sturgeon. Labour can’t afford to wait around for orders from Blair’s wee brother, Keir Starmer. His interest in Scotland is about as shallow as his share of the UK vote.
On everything from Gaza to the two-child benefit cap, fiscal conservatism to private involvement in the NHS, the prime minister is on the wrong side of Scottish political culture. He is yet another well-heeled north London lawyer and his bloviating about English football doesn’t help.
In the past, the Scottish Labour party used to stand proud in Westminster because of the number of ministerial stars that it delivered: Gordon Brown, Donald Dewar, Alistair Darling, George Robertson, Robin Cook. Those days are gone. Most of the 412 Labour MPs are under 45. They have little collective memory of past Labour governments or what it is like to fight Scottish nationalism when it is on a roll.
So, Scottish MPs need to make a bit of noise, and quite soon. Warm words about a new co-operative reset and Scotland being the “beating heart of the UK” will be treated by Scots with the contempt they deserve. They know that there is always tension between Scotland and Westminster — there has to be, because Scotland is always fighting to be heard in the over-centralised UK state. The junior partner in the Union constantly needs to remind Westminster of its existence.
We’re told Starmer has already done his bit by visiting Scotland first and saving Grangemouth. But Grangemouth isn’t saved — far from it. As things stand its Chinese owners and Ineos plan to turn Scotland’s first and largest petrochemical plant, designed to process crude oil from the North Sea, into a receiving port for American liquefied natural gas. Nothing could better exemplify the contradictions of the energy transition. Instead of refining Scottish crude, the plant will be pumping gas produced in America by fracking, a process that is banned in the UK.
Grangemouth could be Labour’s Ravenscraig, the steel plant whose closure 32 years ago drew a line under Scotland as a manufacturing nation. Grangemouth marks the death knell for the oil and gas industry. After all, who needs a petrochemical plant, processing nasty fossil fuels, when we are going full tilt to the green economy? Well, Scottish MPs need to remind the hyperventilating net-zero secretary, Ed Miliband, that 78 per cent of the energy used in the UK is still fossil-based. That isn’t going to change, certainly not in the next six years, despite Miliband’s mission control promising “clean power by 2030”. Labour is going down the same road as the Scottish government five years ago: demonising oil and gas, setting unrealistic targets and ignoring the cost to ordinary families.
Closing down the North Sea prematurely will cost tens of thousands of jobs, make the UK even more dependent on authoritarian regimes such as Qatar and increase domestic energy bills. The Scottish government belatedly realised this and has now turned full circle, equating Labour’s energy policy with Thatcher’s treatment of the miners.
Once they get their feet under the table, Scottish Labour MPs’ first task should be to stop their leaders making the same mistake as Sturgeon: allowing Just Stop Oil to dictate energy policy.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Fears for animal welfare after Met axes wildlife crime unit
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.subtitle: The unit that tackles everything from ivory smuggling to bat protection has been disbanded, leaving only one officer with expertise in the field
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
Only one detective constable with wildlife crime expertise remains at the Metropolitan Police, in a blow for efforts to combat the illegal trade in ivory.
After the Met disbanded its long-standing and well-respected Wildlife Crime Unit (WCU) a fortnight ago, the naturalist Chris Packham led calls for the force to devote more resources to tackling abuse of wildlife.
The police team played a key role in tackling the smuggling of illegal animal parts and plants through Heathrow. Last year it seized thousands of items including snakeskins and live birds at the airport as part of Operation Thunder.
It also played a vital role in enforcing breaches of local wildlife laws, with the housebuilder Bellway Homes fined £600,000 for destroying a bat breeding site four years ago.
However, as part of the New Met for London plan, the WCU was abolished and its two detectives were redeployed to local policing. One of those two officers has subsequently handed in their notice, meaning that when they leave there will be just one detective with significant experience in tackling the illegal wildlife trade.
The Naturewatch Foundation, an animal welfare charity, said it was “shameful” and “short-sighted” to abolish the unit.
“Doing more to tackle serious and organised crime is allegedly a Met Police priority. The wildlife trade is the fourth largest international crime, so why on earth would it axe their highly effective wildlife crime unit?” said Kate Salmon, campaign manager at the group.
The charity is pushing the force to reverse its decision, with more than 600 people signing a petition for a rethink.
“In the whole of the Met there is now only one officer with specialism in wildlife crime, and yet wildlife crime is a globally booming business. Trophies, ivory, exotic animals, not to mention the UK’s own issues,” said Packham.
The broadcaster told The Times: “We all know the police are stretched and need more resources but I’d be happier if they stopped harassing Just Stop Oil and devoted a proportionate amount of time to tackling the abuse of wildlife.”
The WCU’s expertise was both domestic, such as ensuring new building projects followed rules on adding wooded areas and measures such as bat boxes, as well as international, focusing on stopping breaches of the international animal and plant trade treaty, CITES.
News of the WCU being disbanded was revealed internally in the Met about a month ago. The unit was considered crucial to tackling organised wildlife crime, as it worked with intelligence from other government agencies including Border Force and the National Crime Agency. It also partnered with environmental groups including the RSPB and the RSPCA to gather information.
While stopping the trade in illegal plants and animals smuggled into London was one part of its work, another was tackling local issues in parks and green areas. Incidents covered everything from pigeons being kicked in Trafalgar Square to foxes being poisoned and people chopping down trees where birds were nesting.
The team was also responsible for educating borough wildlife officers and providing a central source of information on a highly specialised area.
Those with knowledge of the unit said the main consequence of it being axed was that protection for wildlife crimes would now be less likely.
“Preventing and combating wildlife crime is a global imperative, which the United Kingdom has fully recognised,” said John Scanlon, chairman of the Global Initiative to End Wildlife Crime and the former secretary general of CITES, in a letter to the Met commissioner Sir Mark Rowley.
“Dismantling the Met Wildlife Crime Unit is not only bad for London, and the United Kingdom, but it will impact source countries, and send the wrong message to those who are inclined to engage in wildlife crime.”
While a National Wildlife Crime Unit still exists, it has only an advisory role and, unlike the abolished WCU, is unable to prosecute directly. It means that the RSPCA is one of the only dedicated bodies able to prosecute animal crimes itself.
A spokesperson for the Met said: “Detectives previously attached to the Met’s central wildlife crime unit will now focus on assisting BCUs [basic command units] tackling local crime problems.
“This is in line with our focus on data-driven policing to help keep communities safe. The Met will continue to investigate any allegations of crime involving wildlife.”

https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.title: Anonymous email links Paris rail attacks to far-left group
https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.subtitle: Message about arson attacks is being analysed for links to domestic and international extremists
https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/ar.text:
Investigators are looking into an anonymous email apparently sent by a mysterious ultra-leftist group claiming responsibility for arson attacks on France’s rail network that caused transport chaos hours before the Paris Olympics opening ceremony.
The email was sent to French and international media organisations from an address with the domain name “rise up”. The domain name has been used by violent groups in France in the past, including ultra-leftists, anarchists and radical environmentalists, according to security sources.
However, Gérald Darmanin, the interior minister, said in an interview on Saturday that he could not rule out foreign involvement. He did not name any country but was apparently alluding to Russia, which has allegedly orchestrated arson attacks in several European countries including the UK.
Moscow has been accused of masterminding attempts to destabilise France over the past year, employing low-level agents to carry out nuisance actions and mounting cyberattacks, propaganda and disinformation campaigns. Russia is not represented by a national team at the Paris Olympics, although Russian athletes are competing, and Moscow is angry about President Macron’s support for Ukraine.
A Russian chef with alleged links to the FSB, the Russian intelligence agency, was arrested in Paris on Tuesday and accused of plotting to disrupt the Games.
The arson attacks on Friday damaged signal boxes and fibreoptic cables along lines linking Paris with cities including Lille in the north, Bordeaux in the west and Strasbourg in the east. Eurostar services between Paris and London, Brussels and Amsterdam were also affected.
“Who is responsible? Either it’s from within, or it’s been ordered from abroad,” Darmanin told France 2 television.
• France trains attack: Eurostar and rail network sabotaged — as it happened
Security services are treating the emailed claim of responsibility for the arson attacks seriously, although it is unclear if it is genuine.
“We see [the Games] as a celebration of nationalism, a gigantic staging of the subjugation of peoples by states,” the email read. “Like any great sports event, they are also an opportunity to worship the values that are the foundation of the world of power and money.”
RiseUp, based in the western US city of Seattle, presents itself as a provider of “online communication tools for people and groups working on liberatory social change”. Its website says: “We are a project to create democratic alternatives and practice self-determination by controlling our own secure means of communications.”
The organisation has reportedly failed to respond to past legal orders to reveal the senders of emails.
Its owners are close to “the Italian anarchist movement”, according to French media.
The claim came as police in Paris detained 14 Extinction Rebellion activists accused of planning to “sabotage” the Olympics, Le Parisien newspaper reported. They were aged between 24 and 36.
The movement said it had called off acts of civil disobedience after the arrests. “Our democracy is burning and we are watching the Paris 2024 [Olympic] flame,” it said in a social media post.
French security services said the rail saboteurs’ modus operandi suggested that ultra-leftists were behind the attacks as they had carried out similar strikes on rail infrastructure in France in the past.
Investigators said that media reports about the attacks had been posted on Telegram accounts linked with the far left, although no group previously known to the authorities has claimed responsibility.
SNCF, France’s national rail company, said technicians had been working throughout the weekend to repair the damage and that traffic would return to normal by Monday.
The co-ordinated attacks on high-speed rail lines were precisely targeted to cause maximum disruption and investigators suspect that the arsonists were helped by someone with detailed knowledge of the network.

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Fun-suckers are the real villains in Thelma’s tale
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
The movie Thelma concerns a 93-year-old widow scammed out of her savings who seeks restitution, aided by her wastrel 24-year-old grandson, Danny.
It is a tender, hilarious and sweet (without being saccharine) depiction of the relationship between the very old and their young adult grandkids. Scenes where an endlessly patient Danny schools a frustrated Thelma in computer skills will resonate with many.
It is a paean to the courage of the old, determined to be masters of their destiny despite infuriating infirmities and the loneliness of outliving every friend. Thelma, played by June Squibb, reminds me of my mother: she may remind you of yours. Gen Zs like Danny are depicted as self-pitying, timorous and lost, yet redeemable if given a challenge.
• Thelma review — exquisite hug of a film about a grandma on a mission
So who are the baddies? The middle generation: Thelma’s daughter and son-in-law, Danny’s parents. The ones who worry their grown-up son has lost his wallet or their elderly mother might have a fall. These fun-suckers fret, moan, nag, panic, meddle.
No one loves or even appreciates the “squeezed middle”, tasked until they graduate into Thelmas with shouldering the world.
Fist raised, blood streaking his cheek, head defiantly high as FBI agents try to wrangle him to the ground: that image of Donald Trump after the assassination attempt was emblazoned on Maga campaign merch within hours, an instant icon for the US right.
Yet it electrified Americans far beyond Trump’s base. The Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg described Trump’s response with gleaming eyes as “one of the most badass things I’ve ever seen in my life”. East Coast liberals noted on Twitter/X they felt their patriotism stir.
No citizen is wholly impervious to their nation’s founding myths and here was Trump — the soft-handed, draft-dodging son of a multimillionaire — recast in their minds as frontiersman, flag-raiser at Iwo Jima, General Custer, Rocky Balboa.
But what does that image evoke in those of us beyond America, with no say in this election yet tethered to its global consequences? Queasy horror at the darkness and chaos that is never far from the flags and campaign smiles, fear for the fragility of US democracy and what vengeance Trump could wreak, but mainly shrugging sadness that gun-sick America will never learn.
In Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall you’ll be handed a paintbrush, briefly shown a laminate of Claude Monet’s Water Lilies, and told to join a crowd of people applying acrylic paint to vast canvases. The idea of Colombian artist Oscar Murillo in this project, The Flooded Garden, is for a community to create a 500sq m artwork.
Except it looks … rubbish. Of the 50 or so adults and children dabbing globs of pink and blue to the walls, few were channelling Monet. Some were graffiti-ing their names, others doodling faces or cartoon animals. I had a go myself, trying to summon the garden in Giverny, but just spattered my dress. Then I stood back, hoping to see this collective endeavour in the most favourable light. Nope. Still a mess.
Murillo calls this work a “multi-individual performance”. Yet what it reveals is that an amorphous ad hoc committee won’t create good art. It needs a single visionary, or at least a strict foreman.
After the sentencing of her daughter Cressida to four years in prison, Cathy Gethin gave a speech in which she noted that the 22-year-old, who conspired with Just Stop Oil activists to bring the M25 to a halt, will be unable to attend her brother’s wedding.
Can Mrs Gethin not hear herself? It is hard to construct a purer example of entitlement. The hundreds of thousands of people Cressida and four others helped delay missed funerals, cancer treatments, job interviews, holiday flights.
But these motorway drivers are just normies whose time is worthless, unlike her daughter, self-ordained into a priest caste that divines what random acts will somehow save the planet. Her time is sacred.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/transport/ar.title: Just Stop Oil protesters arrested at Gatwick
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/transport/ar.subtitle: Seven activists removed after trying to block access to the south terminal’s security area during a protest
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/transport/ar.text:
A group of Just Stop Oil protesters who tried to stop passengers at Gatwick have been removed and arrested, the airport said.
Seven members of JSO, an environmental activist group, tried to block access to the south terminal’s central search area where passengers are screened. Video shared by the group showed passengers climbing over the protesters, who had painted orange boxes with them, to enter the security screening area.
Barriers were put up around the protesters and passengers were diverted through a different entrance before the group was removed. There has been no disruption to flights.
A spokesman for the airport said: “London Gatwick is open and operating normally today. There are a small number of protesters at the airport who have now been arrested and are being removed from the airport.”
Last week, ten JSO activists suspected of planning to disrupt Heathrow were arrested. None of the activists had been able to get into the airport, the Metropolitan Police said.
Earlier this month Gatwick became the latest airport to win a High Court injunction to stop would-be environmental activists trespassing on its land.
At a hearing on July 19, lawyers for the airport — the second largest in the UK — sought the court’s protection againsy the “real and imminent risk of blockading, obstruction [and] disruption” at its site near Crawley, West Sussex.
Heathrow, London City, Stansted, Luton, Manchester, East Midlands, Leeds Bradford and Newcastle International airports have all obtained court injunctions against activists in recent weeks.
Police were called to the airport just after 8pm. A spokesman for Sussex police said: “Eight people have been arrested on suspicion of interfering with public infrastructure, and a heightened police presence should be expected at this time.
“The airport is functioning as usual, and no disruption has been caused by protest activity.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Climate protests are virtue signalling, says former National Trust chief
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.subtitle: Sir Simon Jenkins has condemned climate activists who are planning to stage protests at 40 historic properties over the trust’s use of Barclays bank
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
A former chairman of the National Trust has described plans by climate activists to target National Trust estates over its use of Barclays as “virtue signalling”.
Climate activists will hold protests at more than 40 National Trust sites this week in an effort to stop the charity from banking with Barclays, over its links to the fossil fuel industry.
The organisers of the protests, which include staff, volunteers and members of the trust, said that they would not attempt to disrupt overall operations. Instead activists, who are backed by groups such as Extinction Rebellion, Fossil Free London and Christian Climate Action, will focus on creative acts of protest which range from picnics to parades and musical performances.
The actions come after Christian Aid and Oxfam announced that they would stop using Barclays because of its record on climate change.
Sir Simon Jenkins, who served as the chairman of the National Trust from 2008-14, criticised the protests. He said: “These things are so ridiculous and they’re all about posturing and virtue signalling … The National Trust is deeply involved in all forms of conservation and it’s been leading the way in trying to protect the landscape.
“As far as I am concerned it’s been leading the way in which it heats its properties and its energy use and all these things. Its secondary and tertiary links to various activities that other people don’t like is neither here nor there to me.”
Jenkins, the former editor of The Times, expressed support for the National Trust’s position of allowing protests as long as they are peaceful and do not cause damage.
Sally Chapman, a volunteer at National Trust property Knightshayes in Devon, said that she was “really unhappy about the National Trust banking with Barclays”. She added: “I am sure that the National Trust founder Octavia Hill would be too. It does not fit with her vision of providing healthy green spaces for ordinary people.”
Properties that will be targeted include Ham House in West London, Corfe Castle in Dorset, and Chartwell in Kent, the family home and garden of Sir Winston Churchill.
A spokeswoman for the trust said: “The National Trust fully understands the urgency needed to find solutions to the climate crisis and the strength of feeling about this among some of our supporters.
“We welcomed Barclays’ announcement that they will stop direct financing to clients engaged in oil and gas expansion, and that they will require their clients in the energy sector to prepare climate transition plans. It is critically important that we continue to engage with the banking sector to do more and faster to reduce financed emissions.
“We support people’s right to demonstrate, so long as it is done peacefully and it does not damage the historic and natural places we look after.”

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Change? Not in this manifesto of platitudes
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
In the end, perhaps it is an apt image for the whole election. The leader of the Liberal Democrats jumping head-first off a crane, hollering “vote Liberal Democrat!”, his ballooning paunch bouncing up and down on a bungee cord like a prop in a giant game of cup and ball. Here we are again, Britain, taking a leap into the dark, trying to upend the status quo for the third time in a decade (2016, 2019, 2024), only to find within a few years that we are once again spinning in circles, tethered to the same dock.
The previous votes for change were branded more colourfully. Boris Johnson as salesman offered the prospect of “unleashing potential” or “levelling up”, but such dangerous specificity has been shunned by Labour in favour of the more inoffensive and altogether safer catchword: “Change.” This is a stick insect of a political slogan, the campaigning equivalent of staying very, very still and hoping voters focus their critical faculties on the other guy instead.
The other guy can only score, after all, when he’s rigorously pointing out that a stick insect is no substitute for a policy platform. And the record of Rishi Sunak’s own party on the big things — GDP per capita, migration, defence — is so dismal it can bear little scrutiny.
The Tories have been masterfully reinventing themselves as agents of change for 14 years, but that game of dress-up is finally over. In the background, behind the great show, they have presided over the inexorable expansion of a fearsomely useless administrative state; a system in which the pace of change is determined by the technical tussles of bureaucrats and lawyers, where improvements can only ever proceed at the speed of the slowest printer in the building and must always be overwhelmed by the appropriate safeguards and audits.
The result has been a game of policy snakes and ladders. The government declared support for airport expansion, then passed a net zero target guaranteeing anyone trying to build a runway would be stopped in court. Its ministers have stated that only biological women are women, then found their own departments flying transgender pride flags. Our negotiators ruled out European free movement and we wound up with a system that brings in twice as much migration from elsewhere.
What are Labour’s answers to these exercises in futility? Its manifesto is a blur of platitudes, consisting largely of plans to “make the changes we need”, “consider steps” or “explore further measures” in this field or that. There are some concrete proposals, several of which are enough to make one shudder, like plans to establish a parliamentary “modernisation committee” to “drive up standards” or pass a “landmark race equality act” (no doubt based on the “decolonisation” agenda).
Page 16 features a near full-page shot of Sir Keir Starmer staring into the distance before the mighty cliffs of Dover, looking like a McKinsey consultant peeved by the late arrival of his Eurostar. This is the man who, according to self-made legend, used the traditional toolmaking skills of his father to take down a planeful of jihadis single-handedly with just a Biro and an office full of prosecutors. To be fair, there are some sensible ideas in the document. Plans for a retirement age of 80 for the House of Lords would at least ensure that both Joe Biden and soon Donald Trump would be barred from appointment to Britain’s second chamber.
Of course it’s always possible that Starmer is in fact the most brilliant Machiavelli of modern times. This dull lawyer shtick, you see, is really just a front for the real plan to create a clone army of Kate Binghams in a secret laboratory and then to manoeuvre them into key positions running every policy brief from defence procurement to teacher training. Like Margaret Thatcher stockpiling coal before her battle with the miners, perhaps Labour’s modern revolutionary is quietly preparing for his fight with the market-town nimbys of Britain by building a strategic reserve of Bakewell tarts, Shakespeare tickets and saffron. Maybe he’s quietly ready to foment a pitched battle between the soon-to-be dispossessed workers of Scotland’s last oil refinery and the huffing nincompoops of Just Stop Oil. In which case, good luck to the man.
But in truth, Starmer is a creature of this system of judicial power grabs and 21,000-page tax codes. When legal advice arrives telling his policy team they can’t do the things they want to do, or when one of his new “integrity” committees starts telling ministers of the crown how to behave and whom to hire, Starmer’s No 10 will dutifully yield. This, surely, is the essence of Starmerism, insofar as it has any content. It is the steady state that self-styled “centrists” mistake for “grown-up government”.
Meanwhile, there are urgent matters languishing on the national to-do list, like rebuilding our defence and industrial capacity; abolishing wasteful swathes of our university sector and properly funding the critical parts selling themselves to China; replacing the mass importation of cheap workers with fast-track visas for cutting-edge technicians and PhDs; and returning a generation of distressed, smartphone-addicted children to the real world.
One of Labour’s articles of faith is that the Tories have cynically ignored these sorts of problems in favour of relying on mass apathy and base “nationalism” to stay in office. Maybe the mediocre reality is scarier to contemplate — that the Conservatives’ traditional instinct for power has been defeated, landing us with a prime minister whose final campaign gambit is to go on breakfast television with Britain’s “most tattooed mum” and confess his love of sandwiches.
Still, the so-called centrists will now get their wish. A prime minister of their breed with an unassailable majority is about to be installed in Downing Street. Like Emmanuel Macron, without the gold clock and hefty make-up bill, Starmer fancies that he is here to build “a new growth model” and to deliver his country from “nationalism”. That isn’t how it went down in France.
It is easy to blame “populism” for all sorts of ills, but state failure begins with the state. Labour has five years to prove it isn’t just stringing the British public along. But if that doesn’t work out, it will no doubt just go back to the old strategy: finger-wagging at Nigel Farage.

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Just Stop Oil’s idea of justice is a danger to all
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
The co-founder of the Just Stop Oil movement, Roger Hallam, was jailed this month for five years. Judge Christopher Hehir gave four fellow activists four-year jail sentences after they were also found guilty of conspiracy to cause a public nuisance.
During four days in November 2022, the group disrupted the M25 when more than 45 protesters climbed gantries, forcing the police to stop traffic.
The judge said he was handing out exemplary sentences because of the seriousness of these offences and the risk that they would further escalate.
• Prepare for jail, judge tells Just Stop Oil’s Van Gogh protesters
In an interview with The Times, Hallam gloated that the sentences would galvanise further protests. Whether that’s true or not, his attack on the judge is instructive. Hallam believes he should be above the law because he believes that his cause is above the law.
According to him, the world is about to be ended by climate change, which spells “billions of deaths and ecological collapse”. That certainty apparently bestows on Hallam and his ilk an entitlement to behave with no restrictions whatsoever.
This is as chilling as it is preposterous. Whatever may happen in the future, no one has the right to inflict harm on others.
The court heard that the delays caused by the M25 action caused people to miss funerals, flights and exams. A patient suffering from an aggressive cancer missed his appointment. A special-needs child who was late for school missed taking vital medication. The action was intended to produce gridlock throughout southern England, which the judge said would have threatened food supplies and the maintenance of law and order.
That’s why the judge said the evidence for catastrophic climate change was irrelevant. In any event, that evidence is contested. Even scientists who believe that action needs to be taken to mitigate the effects of man-made climate change have nevertheless counselled against wild exaggerations such as the certainty of planetary apocalypse.
For Hallam, however, the argument is as unchallengeable as it is cataclysmic. There is therefore literally nothing that should be ruled out to prevent climate change from happening, because nothing else can compete in importance.
• Will Lloyd: Saintly quest of eco-zealot will lead more astray
After all, according to this thinking, what’s the significance of a cancer patient’s suffering, food supplies or a special-needs child’s uncontrollable behaviour compared to the end of the world and human extinction?
This is a totalitarian perspective that Hallam shares with the great tyrannies of history. For them, the belief that the end justifies the means always derives from the absolutist conviction that there is no alternative to dogmatic certainty about the redemption or perfection of the world.
Today, this drives Islamic extremism; in the past, it helped justify Stalin’s gulags, the French revolutionary terror and the mass murder of heretics by medieval Christians who believed in the imminent end of days and the redemption of humanity.
As Hehir observed of the five defendants: “Each of you some time ago has crossed the line from concerned campaigner to fanatic.” According to Hallam, that proved that the judge himself was a fanatic and “an extreme but predictable example of that psychotic mindset”. Which rather proved the judge’s point.
In an open letter from prison, Hallam wrote: “We should live under the rule of law, and so should the government.” But the rule of law, it appears, is only what meets his approval. For he declared: “The basis of the law is the welfare of the people. If a regime enables the destruction of the lives and livelihoods of the people, then the government is a tyranny, and the people have the right to rebel.”
And he really does believe that the government is planning “the death of its citizens” through its climate change policies. You might have thought that such patently unhinged fanaticism would be viewed as such by all except the most loopy supporters of this cause.
Think again. More than 1,000 celebrities, lawyers and academics, including the Coldplay singer Chris Martin, the former Archbishop of Canterbury Rowan Williams and the artist Dame Tracey Emin signed a letter in which the five jailed activists were said to be “fulfilling a necessary service by alerting the nation to the grave risk we all face”. But they weren’t alerting the nation; they were causing direct and immediate harm to others.
These dignitaries described the sentences passed on the “whole truth five” as “one of the greatest injustices in a British court in modern history”. Really? Some of us might have other candidates for that accolade, such as the sentences passed on the hundreds of innocent postmasters whose lives were destroyed through grotesquely wrongful convictions.
This letter is just the latest example of an alarming cultural slide. We saw it over the Occupy movement when people in public life saying “Well, they do have a point about the iniquities of capitalism” helped sanitise Occupy’s violent and unlawful activities.
We saw it when police officers took the knee in support of Black Lives Matter despite its aggressive anti-police agenda, and when Sir Keir Starmer and Angela Rayner even tweeted a picture of themselves doing so.
And now we can see that, just like Roger Hallam, 1,000 of the great and the good believe that an opinion they share should trump judicial decisions. Such people, it seems, believe less in convictions under the rule of law than in disorder under the rule of convictions.

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/letters.title: Times letters: Ensuring the lessons of Covid-19 are learnt
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/letters.text:
Sir, Your leading article (“Be Prepared”, Jul 19) is right to welcome the recommendations from Baroness Hallett’s report on Covid preparedness. Her ten-point plan is a good framework for addressing the shortcomings exposed during the pandemic. However, many inquiry reports over the past two decades have similarly urged government to review crisis preparedness, and far too little has been done to ensure that lessons really are learnt.
Crises will happen, and not only pandemics, and they are by definition unpredictable; proper planning and preparedness is needed to mitigate their effects. Any crisis demands a speedy response based on tried and regularly tested systems. Decisions should then be made on the basis of best available scientific advice.
The recommendations from the Covid inquiry will be sure to be implemented only if the prime minister takes a personal lead in overseeing that implementation. He should demand regular reports from all departments and agencies. The single independent statutory body on crisis preparedness proposed by Lady Hallett must report regularly to the prime minister, not to his officials.Alun Evans Secretary, Foot and Mouth Disease: Lessons Learned Inquiry
Sir, Lady Hallett’s report on the UK’s pandemic preparedness and resilience says that little attention was paid to the experience of Sars, an earlier novel coronavirus, in east Asia (“Poor planning and groupthink failed public, Covid inquiry says”, Jul 19). It also indicates that some scientific advisers did not know how far their advice was being acted on, if it was acted on at all.
In South Korea and Taiwan, through a combination of early border restrictions, localised lockdowns, strict testing, contact tracing and quarantining, Covid-19 could be contained before a vaccine was found. What Lady Hallett’s report omits is the reorganisation done by the South Korean government in response to its poor management of the earlier MERS-CoV outbreak. It decided to share executive powers on pandemic management between politicians, administrators, public health speciACalists and scientists to optimise decision-making. In a fast-moving pandemic, all that expertise is needed in real time to stay ahead of the curve.
In the UK the prime minister has substantial executive powers. As a country we are dependent on his or her competence in critical decision making and ability to choose between difficult options to manage a crisis. The physical and mental demands on any prime minister and cabinet during a pandemic are probably unsustainable, but we experienced a total failure of our government system. We need to consider a radical reform of pandemic preparedness, embedding public health specialists and scientists along with politicians directly in the decision-making process. Professor Ian Kunkler Edinburgh
Sir, Reading about Lady Hallett’s report, I found myself thinking about the parallels between the pandemic and the physical defence of our nation. Quite rightly, Lady Hallett identified as shortcomings our collective avoidance of inconvenient truths and our underinvestment in preparing for the next, inevitable, crisis. Our inability to grasp such nettles is mirrored in how we have disinvested in our physical security and defence as well. Perhaps it is now time to fully address the first duty of any government — which is all aspects of security and defence of the nation — whatever the cost. Bruce WilliamsRear admiral, ret’d Kingsbridge, Devon
Sir, Sir Muir Gray is correct to suggest (letter, Jul 18) that there are opportunities to cut waste in the NHS by reducing prescribing. The estimated 10 per cent of drugs, equating to 110 million items, that may be unnecessarily prescribed in primary care was a key finding of the 2021 report on overprescribing, which I led on behalf of the Department of Health and Social Care. Although medicines can be life-saving, they can also be harmful and can be wasted. Our report recommended the expansion of clinical pharmacists in general practice, and increasing social prescribing. There is also huge potential for evidence-based, digital therapeutics recommended by National Institute for Health and Care Excellence that provide self-guided cognitive behavioural therapy as a safe alternative to potentially harmful hypnotics for common mental health conditions such as insomnia. Scotland has shown how this can be done; England should not be left behind.Dr Keith RidgeChief pharmaceutical officer for England 2006-22
Sir, To the types of waste described by Sir Muir Gray we ought to add “rework”, doing something again (and perhaps again) because it was not done correctly the first time. Rework is endemic in the NHS, but a study in 2019 showed that hardly any trusts recognised the problem or measured the associated costs. Rework is the cost of poorly designed and inconsistently implemented processes. Not only do these inflict huge hidden but avoidable costs on and waste valuable and scarce resources, they also place no value on patients’ time. John M EvansOrganisational psychologistHeathfield, E Sussex
Sir, Sir Muir Gray and your other correspondents on improving the NHS are drifting away from the need for immediate action in favour of long-term planning, but I am an octogenarian, and my medical needs cannot wait for the fruition of all the sensible thought being proposed. Dr Surinder Bakhshi Birmingham
Sir, I applaud the punishments meted out to the JSO leaders (“Record five-year jail term for Just Stop Oil’s founder”, Jul 19). I fully agree with their arguments but their methods have been selfish and confrontationist. The sentences are not against free speech, but against disruption and vandalism. They can still protest, but now perhaps with more thought for their fellow citizens. Ian Powick Hagley, Worcs
Sir, Why fill our overcrowded prisons with the Just Stop Oil activists? A far more apt punishment would be long hours of community service working to improve the environment. Viv MercerSouthport
Sir, Dale Vince says that the sentences given to the members of Extinction Rebellion, who disrupted the M25 for days and misbehaved in court, make the UK akin to “North Korea and Russia” (“Donor urges PM to free JSO five”, Jul 19). He says that the court, which has examined all the evidence, should be overruled by the government — this is precisely what would make the UK like North Korea and Russia.Ray Bowden London N14
Sir, Andrew Bano suggests (letter, Jul 19) veterans’ courts as a means of ensuring that former military personnel are given sentences properly mitigated by the effects of service in the armed forces. As an ex-soldier, I am as concerned about the creep of veteran exceptionalism. Seeking to shield serving and former military personnel from the law has a counter-productive, infantilising effect. It undermines aspects of the moral component of service, and causes some veterans to see themselves as more deserving members of society. That doesn’t help with reintegration into civilian life.
Defendants in criminal courts are sentenced on evidence, gravity of crime, criminal records and mitigation. It may be that improvements can be found in bringing service mitigation to bear at trial, but a separate court system is morally and legally indefensible.Michael GillSutton Coldfield
Sir, Juliet Samuel (“Net-zero energy may leave us with no power”, Jul 18) acknowledges the recent gas crisis, which has led to high prices, crushing inflation and energy security issues, but goes on to argue for continued reliance on fossil fuel imports. Ember’s independent analysis, based on whole-system modelling, shows that having homegrown renewable generation and storage cuts our reliance on imports and improves our energy security. Electrified heat and transport will cut import reliance further. We live in volatile times; UK renewables blunted the impact of the recent gas crisis, and they will unshackle us from the next one.Frankie MayoSenior UK analyst, Ember
Sir, Lord Robertson of Port Ellen is right that we must take managing our relationship with Beijing seriously (“Defence review chief sounds China alert”, Jul 16). China is the biggest foreign policy challenge we face. The new government’s commitment to Aukus and its proposed China audit across Whitehall is welcome, though it remains to be seen whether they indicate a wider commitment to embrace the Indo-Pacific tilt.
There is merit in taking a more co-ordinated approach with European allies. A unified front would be much more likely to influence Beijing, which — for this reason — prefers to deal with other countries bilaterally. Varying policies on China in Europe makes a joined-up approach difficult, but with a second Trump presidency increasingly likely the continent must become more co-ordinated if it is to guarantee its long-term security.Connor HorsfallLondon SW1A
Sir, You report (“I lived on ‘Mars’ for a year. This is what it was like”, Jul 19) that a “psychological predisposition to interpersonal conflict is among the characteristics Nasa looks to screen out during the selection process [for astronauts]”. The same is true of submariners, who may have to spend six months in unavoidable contact with others. They tend to be the most affable characters. Matthew Hudson Woodburn (next to the Faslane naval base), Argyll
Sir, Donald Trump says that he survived the assassination attempt because God was on his side. One can only wonder what he thinks God had against Corey Comperatore, the man who was killed.Ron Jacobs Farnham, Surrey
Sir, The remark by one of Oscar Wilde’s characters about the House of Lords (letter, Jul 19) reminded me of WS Gilbert’s satirical view of the British political system from the same era, as demonstrated in Iolanthe. In the operetta, a peer comments that “When Wellington thrashed Bonaparte/ As every child can tell/ The House of Peers, throughout the war/ Did nothing in particular/ And did it very well.”Amanda LuntChichester
Sir, Janice Turner’s comment that the smartphone has replaced so many documents necessary to life (Notebook, Jul 18) reminded me of when, at 80, I decided to be modern and changed my apps to fingerprint access instead of passwords. Wonderful, until I visited New York and left my phone at Heathrow. It was significantly less convenient to access my documents with my digit 3,000 miles away. Kenneth WatersSouthwold, Suffolk

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.title: Hundreds of celebrities rail against ‘injustice’ of Just Stop Oil sentences
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.subtitle: Just Stop Oil activists were given four and five-year sentences over 2022 stunt that brought M25 motorway to a standstill
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.text:
More than 1,100 lawyers, celebrities, academics and artists have called for an urgent meeting with the attorney-general to address the “injustice” of the sentences handed to five environmental activists for peaceful protest.
Roger Hallam, 58, was last week jailed for five years for co-ordinating the protest that disrupted the M25 in London over four days in 2022, during which 45 protesters climbed gantries on the motorway, forcing police to stop traffic. Daniel Shaw, 38, Lucia Whittaker de Abreu, 35, Louise Lancaster, 58, and Cressida Gethin, 22, were each given four years after being found guilty along with Hallam of conspiracy to cause a public nuisance.
The jail terms, handed down by Judge Christopher Hehir, exceed those given to two Just Stop Oil activists who scaled the Queen Elizabeth II Bridge over the Dartford Crossing in October 2022.
Last week the prime minister faced calls to intervene in the case of the activists, known as the Whole Truth Five, while the United Nations human rights commissioner described the term as “deeply troubling” and “disproportionate”. Dale Vince, the millionaire Labour donor, and Chris Packham, the naturalist and broadcaster, called for a meeting with the attorney-general, with Packham describing the sentence as a “grotesque miscarriage of justice”.
In a letter to the attorney-general, more than 1,100 people, including Rowan Williams, the former Archbishop of Canterbury, Sir Geoffrey Bindman KC, one of the country’s most distinguished human rights lawyers, and the artist Dame Tracey Emin echoed the call by Vince and Packham.
The letter, which is also signed by Sir David King, the former chief scientific adviser, Chris Martin, the Coldplay frontman, and Sir Philip Pullman, the author of the His Dark Materials trilogy, described the sentencing as “one of the greatest injustices in a British court in modern history”.
Other signatories to the letter, shared with The Times, include Packham, the celebrity chef Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall, Toby Jones, the star of Mr Bates vs The Post Office, Danny Boyle, the Trainspotting director, Lord Cashman, the actor and LGBT campaigner, and Annie Lennox, the singer and activist.
“With prisons at breaking point and the new government acting urgently to address this, how can these sentences be seen as anything other than insanity? The sentences, ranging from four to five years, are higher than those given to many who commit serious sexual assault,” the letter says.
“The defendants were denied the right to explain to a jury why they took the action they did, making a mockery of the right to a fair trial, with the judge saying that the Crown Prosecution’s agreed facts on climate collapse — including that the world has gone beyond 1.5C for 12 consecutive months — were neither here nor there.”
The letter says the five activists were “fulfilling a necessary service by alerting the nation to the grave risk we all face”, with scientists expressing fears that the Earth is already at “breaking point”.
“The world stands at a crossroads and so does our democracy. We write in support of Chris Packham and Dale Vince’s request for an urgent meeting with you, to be recorded so it is transparent to the public, to discuss the jailing of truth tellers and their silencing in court,” the letter concludes.
The trial at Southwark crown court was told that the M25 protest caused economic damage of £765,000, while the cost to the Metropolitan Police was more than £1.1 million. The protests were also said to have affected more than 700,000 vehicles and left the M25 “compromised” for at least 120 hours.
Hallam and the others will not qualify for early release after 40 per cent of their time is served, as the emergency release scheme is in place for only 18 months and will expire before they qualify.
On Monday, JSO confirmed that it would be taking action at airports this summer after the government did not accede to demands to sign a legally binding treaty to stop the extraction and burning of oil, gas and coal by 2030. The new campaign was first revealed by The Times last month.
Last week Gatwick became the latest major airport to secure a High Court injunction to stop environmental activists from trespassing on its land, joining airports such as London City, Manchester and East Midlands Airport.
The letter to the attorney-general came as a civil liberties group said that it would engage in talks with the government to resolve a legal battle over the way protests are policed in the UK.
Liberty won a legal challenge against the Home Office in May over protest regulations passed by statutory instrument last year when Suella Braverman was the home secretary. The measures lowered the threshold for what is considered “serious disruption” to community life, from “significant” and “prolonged” to “more than minor”.
The department had failed to carry out a fair consultation process, the High Court ruled, and the measures were quashed. An appeal was due to be heard in London on Tuesday but the hearing was adjourned at the eleventh hour after Liberty said the group is to hold talks with Yvette Cooper, the home secretary, as the parties seek to “find a resolution in the case”.
Separately, two JSO supporters in their eighties on Monday denied damaging property after the protective glass surrounding the Magna Carta at the British Library was allegedly attacked in May. The Rev Dr Sue Parfitt, 82, and Judith Bruce, 85, each pleaded not guilty to a charge of damaging property, when they appeared at Wood Green crown court in north London.
