https://www.thetimes.com/article/times-l.title: Times letters: Disquiet over loss of winter fuel allowance
https://www.thetimes.com/article/times-l.text:
Sir, As a recipient of the winter fuel allowance I applaud the chancellor’s decision to cancel the payment that would otherwise be arriving in my bank account in November solely because of my date of birth — another example of ageism (“Tax rise hints as chancellor cuts winter fuel payment”, Jul 30). But I hope the requisitioned winter fuel payments of people like me do not vanish into the £22 billion black hole. Instead they should be put into a winter warmth budget for the many thousands of people who will be dreading the winter, many of whom will be admitted to hospital with hypothermia, adding to the financial pressures on the NHS.Sir Muir GrayDirector, the Optimal Ageing Programme, Oxford
Sir, Without doubt there will be many unnecessary deaths this winter. The pensioner generation, which abhors debt, would rather “go without” heating when winter comes along. Hence the withdrawal of the heating allowance will see them into an early grave — with the consequence of fewer state pensions having to be paid. Is this actually slow death by stealth? How a country cares for its elderly is a measure of its humanity.Sheila HarringtonRickmansworth, Herts
Sir, It seems short-sighted to remove the winter fuel allowance for ten million pensioners. There are many people who are just about managing on their state pension who rely on the allowance to get through the winter, especially as fuel prices are still high. I expect more people will have to apply for means-tested benefits as a result. The government could have made a start by removing the £10 Christmas bonus, which did mean something when it was introduced in 1972.Pam BucknallHorsham, W Sussex
Sir, Pensioners struggling with winter heating bills; Alzheimer’s sufferers needing long-term social care; parents of children with autism or ADHD who have felt obliged to remove them from state schools that were failing them and put them into private schools. These are the people upon whom Labour has chosen to place the burden of repairing the public finances. The nasty party indeed.Richard ParlourLincoln
Sir, You report (Jul 30) that Rachel Reeves is expected to announce a royal commission on the future of social care. She could save much time and expense by resurrecting the Dilnot Commission of 2011. When Theresa May attempted to enact some of its provisions, the Labour Party (and indeed some of her own party) labelled it a “dementia tax” and the proposals were promptly shelved for reasons of political expediency. Dilnot’s report offers a far quicker solution than a royal commission.Edward StainesBrancepeth, Co Durham
Sir, Rachel Reeves said that it is impossible to make changes “unless you can say where the money is going to come from”. Perhaps we can learn from European countries with more advanced social care systems, such as Ireland, France and Germany, which are making headway by making care costs tax-deductible. This promotes care equity, fairness and financial relief for individuals, encourages formal care employment practices and eases pressure on government-funded services such as the NHS.Jody O’NeillCEO, Curam care providers
Sir, Melanie Phillips, arguing that disruptive climate protests are illegitimate, writes: “Even scientists who believe that action needs to be taken to mitigate the effects of man-made climate change have nevertheless counselled against wild exaggerations such as the certainty of planetary apocalypse” (“Just Stop Oil’s idea of justice is a danger to all”, Jul 30). She names no names and sets the bar at an absurdly high level, as if we are not entitled to act unless we can show that human extinction is assured. But anyone who is attending to the daily litany of new temperature records and extreme weather events can see where we are heading unless we take extreme evasive action — the “rapid, deep and immediate” cuts to greenhouse gas emissions called for by the scientific community of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Phillips claims that “the end justifies the means” is the creed of dictators, revolutionaries and religious fanatics. In fact, as she knows, the weighing of ends and means is the daily business of government.Professor Jason Scott-WarrenCambridge
Sir, I accept that our climate is changing and that mankind is helping it along. However, if the British Isles sank into the North Sea tonight it would not make any difference to climate change worldwide. If activists want to make a difference, they should demonstrate in the US, China, India, Russia and Japan, the countries that burn the most oil.Chris BryantWinscombe, Somerset
Sir, Although I believe that everyone in UK should be able to speak the king’s English, I also think that local dialects are an important part of our heritage and should be maintained and celebrated. The error made by North Yorkshire council in its litter campaign slogan, “Gerrit in’t bin” (letter and news, Jul 29), has little to do with lack of understanding of the Yorkshire dialect and everything to do with an all too common ignorance of punctuation rules.Linda DaviesNorth Wootton, Somerset
Sir, You report (Jul 30) that the chancellor now proposes to start charging VAT on school fees from January rather than, as was expected, at the beginning of the 2025 school year in September. The timing of this new levy, mid-year, tends to support the view that the policy is driven by the politics of spite, as it will be complicated in January for the state sector to accommodate those children whose parents have to withdraw them from private schools; it will be damaging to those private schools; and most importantly it will be harmful to the children themselves to make this switch mid-year, especially if it takes place a term before public exams. The prime minister promised government “unburdened by doctrine”, which I had perhaps optimistically hoped would mean his administration shunning the more malicious policies of socialist dogma. This tax, and its timing, would appear to break that promise.James BlountBlandford Forum, Dorset
Sir, Professor David Jacques considers the government’s cancellation of the Stonehenge tunnel scheme “joyous news” (Jul 30) but for many like me it is a grave disappointment. Cancelling Winterbourne Stoke’s bypass condemns it to the continued blight of thousands of vehicles a day on a single carriageway severing the village; rat-running will continue through nearby Shrewton. The A303 near Stonehenge will remain an accident blackspot; and traffic jams will carry on infuriating drivers and hampering economic growth in the southwest. Not moving forward with the scheme is the government’s prerogative, but doing nothing is not an option.Peter SaundersFormer curator, Salisbury Museum
Sir, We have just arrived home, having passed Stonehenge some hours ago at less than 5mph, with east-bound traffic at a standstill. The West Country deserved better than this decision. So much for the government’s mantra about infrastructure.Richard DaveyMiddle Lambrook, Somerset
Sir, In your obituary of Edna O’Brien (July 29) you allude to copies of her first novel, The Country Girls, being “ceremoniously burnt” because it offended Irish morals. This “book-burning” episode has been headlined in almost every British publication but no witness or evidence of the event has ever been forthcoming. In 2015 Father Tom Stack, a priest I knew, wrote a series of letters to The Irish Times seeking any witness, or any evidence from anyone who had information about this alleged book-burning. He was supported in this quest by Professor John Horgan, then head of media studies at Dublin City University. Stack travelled to Co Clare and investigated every possible source but no evidence was ever produced, and no witness (even under cover of anonymity) ever came forward. O’Brien, whom I knew, was hurt by the rebuffs she initially received from her own community, but she admitted later at interview that “maybe it was just a very small fire”. Even so, no confirmation has been available. Until we have some evidence that this sensational book-burning occurred, we should treat the episode as legend rather than fact.Mary KennyDeal, Kent
Sir, Jonathan Romain may be right that the rehabilitation of criminals could prevent reoffending (“Don’t cheer the Olympic rapist but do let him compete”, Jul 29). However, representing one’s country in the Olympics (or in any international competition) is a huge honour that should not be offered to anyone guilty of such a crime as Steven van de Velde, however remorseful he may be, and however good at his sport. Giving him the chance to put on his country’s vest makes light of both his crime and his victim’s ordeal.Dr Sarah NachshenLondon NW11
Sir, An obvious omission from the list of best film scores is Rachmaninov’s haunting Second Piano Concerto, which runs through the whole of Brief Encounter (1945) and is the perfect background to Celia Johnson’s beautifully articulated soliloquies.Angela LynneShropham, Norfolk
Sir, Emma Duncan (Notebook, Jul 30) is right about the value of memoirs to future generations. I would add only that it is best to get down to the writing while the memory is relatively fresh, as time plays tricks with the mind. I wrote my published memoir A Road Less Travelled aged 68 to see if I could write a book. As a result I had seven more published in my seventies. Now aged 81, I would not start on a memoir out of choice.Robin KnightLondon W4
Sir, Further to your story “Lettuce is a little gem for nettle stings” (Jul 30), surely the value of the dock leaf in reducing the effect of nettle stings is that dock often grows alongside nettles in the wild. You’d struggle to find a lettuce in an average hedgerow.Philip DownerTeddington, Middx
Sir, I once had to meet the broadcaster and astronomer Sir Patrick Moore off a train to take him to a work-related dinner. When his train drew in I shook his hand (Feedback, Jul 27; letters, Jul 29 & 30). His response was: “Congratulations, you have just shaken the only hand that will ever have shaken hands with Orville Wright, Charles Lindburgh, Yuri Gagarin, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin.”Edward AllhusenMoretonhampstead, Devon
Sir, I concur with the sentiment of Lorna Stather’s letter (“Line of duty”, Jul 29): I, too, feel comforted to see washing drying in the open air. When visiting my family in Florida I asked why washing was always dried in the tumble dryer, only to be told: “It dries too quickly outdoors.” I am still baffled by that answer.Deanne ClayShipston-on-Stour, Warks

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Police fear Just Stop Oil jail sentences will spark more protests
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.subtitle: The record term for Roger Hallam could serve as a ‘rallying call’, says the detective who led the investigation into his plot to bring the M25 to a standstill
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
The record jail sentence for the co-founder of Just Stop Oil could serve as a “rallying call” to other climate activists for a wave of protests, police believe.
Roger Hallam, 58, was jailed for five years on Thursday for orchestrating protests that disrupted the M25 over four days in November 2022 when 45 protesters climbed gantries on various parts of the motorway, forcing police to stop traffic.
Daniel Shaw, 38, Lucia Whittaker De Abreu, 35, Louise Lancaster, 58, and Cressida Gethin, 22, were each given four years after being found guilty along with Hallam of conspiracy to cause a public nuisance.
The sentences, handed down by Judge Christopher Hehir, are thought to be the longest ever given for peaceful protest and have been widely criticised.
The prime minister is facing calls to repeal the raft of anti-protest laws that were introduced by the Conservatives over the past two years.
Detective Inspector Chris Rudd, who led the investigation, said there were “certainly signals from the [activist] groups” that they intended to stage a protest in retaliation to the sentences.
He told The Times: “The judge commented upon sentencing that he hoped it may have some deterrent effect on others that wanted to cause serious disruption to members of the public. I do hope it does have some deterrent effect. But for some, it might be a rallying call.”
The five ­Just Stop Oil activists were recorded by an undercover reporter for The Sun during a Zoom call in which they discussed the planned ­protests and were aiming to recruit others.
They were sentenced under legislation introduced by the previous government to get tougher on disruptive tactics used by ­environmental protesters, including blocking roads and attacks on sporting events. A United Nations human rights commissioner condemned the measures as “deeply troubling” and “disproportionate”.
Rudd, who oversees most environmental protests in London, said the protesters were known to police before the covert recording. “There is mention of this being a simple Zoom call resulting in people ending up in prison for five years, but to be absolutely clear: the call contained compelling evidence of them engaging in a plan to conduct what is criminal activity. They wanted to cause absolute gridlock and chaos.”
During the trial, Metropolitan Police officers were stationed at court to deal with disruption from the defendants.
Rudd said less than 10 per cent of Just Stop Oil activists who appear in court plead guilty, compared with about 50 per cent in groups such as Extinction Rebellion, whose members followed the “longstanding tradition” of protesters “taking [punishment] on the chin”.
He added: “Most [Just Stop Oil activists] will self-represent at trial, making the trial process much longer. And as we’ve seen recently, make the trial itself a protest ground.”
The court was told that the M25 protests delayed more than 700,000 vehicles and caused economic damage of £765,000, and the cost to the Met was more than £1.1 million.
Hallam and the others will not qualify for early release after 40 per cent of their time is served as the emergency scheme is only in place for 18 months and will expire before they qualify.
• Labour announces early release for 5,500 prisoners
Lord Falconer of Thoroton, the former justice secretary and lord chancellor, has said the sentences make him feel “very uncomfortable”.
He said: “I am not criticising the judge because I am sure the judge is going with whatever the sentencing guidelines are. But these are people who are not violent criminals.
“They cause enormous irritation to a large number of people. However, to be sentencing people to four and five years in prison for that is maybe an indication as to why the prisons are so full. Maybe prison was appropriate, I don’t dispute that — but for that length of time, I feel uncomfortable at that. But there can be an appeal.”
John McDonnell, the former shadow chancellor, said: “Post Office destroys lives, water companies pollute our rivers, [the Criminal Cases Review Commission] leaves innocent people to rot in prison, Covid ministers’ incompetence costs thousands of lives, but nobody is punished. Stop traffic on M25 and get five years in prison. This is brutally unjust.”
Sir Robert Buckland, the former Tory justice secretary, said the sentences were “fully justified and entirely merited”.
He said: “I hope it sends a very clear message to self-appointed campaigners that they have to be held accountable for their actions as well, just like everyone else and they are not above the law. There is a silent majority who are fed up with random forms of protest that cause widespread disruption. We’re law-abiding people in this country who want to be protected.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/media/articl.title: Eco tycoon could silence Guido Fawkes blog in defamation case
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/media/articl.subtitle: Dale Vince, the millionaire and Labour Party donor, is suing the political website’s editor over its reports of his comments regarding the Israel-Gaza conflict
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/media/articl.text:
A political blog faces a landmark legal attempt to block it from view in the UK as part of a row prompted by a millionaire eco businessman and Labour donor.
Dale Vince, a former funder of the activist group Just Stop Oil, is suing the editor of the Guido Fawkes blog for defamation over its reports on comments the businessman made regarding the Israel-Gaza conflict.
Last October, Vince, 62, told Times Radio that “one man’s terrorist is another man’s freedom fighter” — a comment that triggered a barrage of criticism, including from Angela Rayner, who is now the deputy prime minister.
At the time, Vince was being interviewed at the Labour party conference in Liverpool in the immediate aftermath of Hamas’s attack on Israel and before the country had retaliated.
The millionaire founder of Ecotricity had just switched his political support from Just Stop Oil to Labour, and was responding to a question about his reaction to Sir Keir Starmer’s pronouncement that his support for Israel was unequivocal.
Some five months later at a Westminster lunch, journalists reminded Rayner of Dale’s comments and she described them as “appalling”.
Vince, who is said to have donated £5 million to Labour since 2014, has settled claims with a broadcaster, a Fleet Street newspaper and three former Conservative MPs over coverage of his comments.
The Times understands that lawyers for the entrepreneur, who is estimated to be worth about £107 million, have been granted permission by the High Court to issue proceedings against the blog’s editor, Paul Staines, for defamation.
He is also suing Lord Bailey of Paddington, the Conservative peer and former London mayoralty candidate, and Richard Tice, the deputy leader of the Reform Party.
Proceedings against Staines must be served in Ireland, where the blog is based. If the libel claim succeeds, it is understood that Vince will consider asking the judge for a “blocking order” if Staines refuses to remove the critical comments from his website.
That would be a novel legal move. The orders on websites are normally used in intellectual property cases to block the streaming of pirate media feeds, for example, in issues around Premier League football and streamed films.
However, lawyers note that the High Court’s power to grant a blocking order is not limited to copyright cases and it is speculated that in the case of a defamation finding, there is nothing to prevent a successful claimant from obtaining an order. It is anticipated that the defendant will refuse to remove content.
Blocking orders are directed at internet service and broadband providers.
While the Defamation Act 2013 gives judges the power to order web hosting services to remove content, enforcing those rulings can be difficult in cases where a website is hosted overseas.
Therefore, lawyers have pointed out that in those cases, a blocking order is likely to be the only way of forcing a losing defendant in a libel claim to remove the offending content.
Staines has said that he will defend the claim and has told The Times that Vince’s claim has “obvious implications for freedom of speech”.
The 57-year-old blogger accused Vince of “attempting a Slapp [a strategic lawsuit against public participation]” to intimidate critics”.
Comparing the Labour donor to Russian oligarchs, Staines said he was “using his wealth and power to bully opposition politicians and other political critics”.
Both Bailey — who is being sued for comments he made in a broadcast — and Tice are also defending Vince’s claims.
All three claims are being heard separately. Jonathan Coad, the solicitor acting for Bailey, said that the Tory peer would “vigorously defend” Vince’s claim, which he said was an “assault on his right to freedom of speech”.
Staines said that “the only reason” that Vince was suing him and Bailey as individuals was “to intimidate us with the threat of personal bankruptcy. Neither Shaun nor I are the type to bend the knee to bullies”.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Prepare for jail, judge tells Just Stop Oil’s Van Gogh protesters
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.subtitle: Phoebe Plummer and Anna Holland convicted after damaging Sunflowers frame at the National Gallery
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
Two Just Stop Oil activists have been found guilty of criminal damage after they threw tomato soup at a Van Gogh painting in the National Gallery and damaged its antique frame.
Phoebe Plummer and Anna Holland, both 22, threw two tins of Heinz tomato soup at Sunflowers and then glued themselves to the wall in October 2022.
Although the painting, which was completed in 1888 and is worth up to £72.5 million, was protected by a glass cover, the 17th-century Italian frame was damaged by the soup, which acted like paint stripper, Southwark crown court was told. Prosecutors believe the soup may have caused £10,000 in damage to the frame.
The pair, who denied damaging property, showed no emotion as the jury announced its verdict after a four-day trial. Judge Christopher Hehir released them on bail before their sentencing on September 27. Hehir told the activists to come to court “prepared in practical and emotional terms to go to prison on that date”.
The maximum sentence for the offence is ten years’ imprisonment. The bail conditions stipulate that they must not carry glue, paint or any adhesive substance in a public place and must not visit any galleries or museums.
The court was told that the pair had visited the museum a day before the incident to carry out reconnaissance and bought the tins of soup from a supermarket.
In a statement read to the jury, Isabella Kocum, a frame conservator, said she was “shocked and dismayed by the extent of corrosion this tomato soup” caused to the “exquisite antique frame”.
She told the court: “The frame was specifically chosen for Van Gogh’s painting because of the matching colouration. I remain amazed at how corrosive the soup was to the frame. Even once the majority of the soup had been removed, I was alarmed to see that the remainder was acting like a paint stripper in front of my eyes.”
Plummer, who studied at the University of Manchester and represented herself at the trial, told the court that she decided to use tomato soup “because it would stand out” and that it “symbolised the link between the climate crisis and the cost of living crisis”.
The two activists denied that they considered the frame when planning and carrying out the protest and told the court that they believed the painting would be protected by the glass cover.
Plummer and Holland said they were taking instructions from someone else in Just Stop Oil but refused to identify the person.
• Hundreds of celebrities rail against ‘injustice’ of Just Stop Oil sentences
Plummer told the jury: “I love that painting. I know it is a valuable, precious thing. That is why it is protected… I didn’t think about the frame. I have never heard of anyone going to a gallery to look at frames and not the paintings they encase… I didn’t think the members of the public who gasped were thinking about the frame either.”
In her closing speech, Plummer claimed that she was “sounding an alarm bell” on climate change and invoked the example of the suffragettes and the civil rights movement in the United States.
She said: “I don’t think that action like this fits the black and white letter of the law. Sometimes morality is different from the law, different from justice, different from legal directions. We caused some damage to the frame. The painting was returned to the gallery the same day. The frame has not been further restored since then.
“The frame was not damaged enough to warrant further restoration. It is still deemed worthy to encase a precious, priceless work of art. I intended to shine a light on the climate crisis and on the cost of living crisis.
After the trial, Katie McFadden from the law firm Hodge Jones & Allen, who represented Holland, said she was “extremely disappointed” with the decision and that they would consider whether to appeal against the conviction.
It came as ten Just Stop Oil activists were charged with conspiracy to disrupt Heathrow. All ten were arrested at the airport on Wednesday, police said. They appeared at Westminster magistrates’ court, where eight were remanded in custody.
Both took place against the backdrop of five Just Stop Oil activists being handed record sentences for peaceful protest last week.
Roger Hallam, 58, was jailed for five years for co-ordinating a protest that disrupted the M25 in London over four days in 2022, during which 45 protesters climbed gantries on the motorway, forcing police to stop traffic.
Daniel Shaw, 38, Lucia Whittaker De Abreu, 35, Louise Lancaster, 58, and Cressida Gethin, 22, were each given four years after being found guilty along with Hallam of conspiracy to cause a public nuisance.
The jail terms, handed down by Hehir, exceed those given to two Just Stop Oil activists who scaled the Queen Elizabeth II Bridge over the Dartford Crossing in October 2022.
Last week Sir Keir Starmer faced calls to intervene in the case of the activists, known as the Whole Truth Five, while the United Nations human rights commissioner described the terms as “deeply troubling” and “disproportionate”.
